\section{Metallic threshold classification and the Fischer cover}\label{sec:metallic-cover}

We now classify the overlap threshold throughout the constant-type metallic
quadratic Pisot-unit family.  The golden system is the unique member whose
nontrivial threshold is three: every parameter $A\ge2$ is invertible at every
aperture $m\ge2$.  We prove this first as a finite-block bijection theorem and
then pass to the two-sided SFT conjugacy.  A dynamical-zeta defect detects the
single golden branch at aperture two.  We finally identify the canonical
right-resolving presentation of the Fibonacci image shift in the presented
stabilized alphabet.

\subsection{The metallic two-window boundary}

\begin{definition}[Boundary-modified constant-type rank data]\label{def:metallic-window-data}
Fix an integer $A\ge 1$ and define the metallic quadratic Pisot unit
\[
\beta_A:=\frac{A+\sqrt{A^2+4}}2.
\]
It is the positive root of $x^2-Ax-1$, and its algebraic conjugate is
$-\beta_A^{-1}$, of modulus less than one.  Define
\[
Q_0^{(A)}:=1,\qquad Q_1^{(A)}:=A+1,\qquad
Q_{j+2}^{(A)}:=A Q_{j+1}^{(A)}+Q_j^{(A)}.
\]
This is the metallic recurrence associated with the continued-fraction tail
$[A,A,\ldots]$, shifted so that the golden case $A=1$ gives
$Q_j^{(1)}=F_{j+2}$.
Let
\[
\mathcal A_A:=\{0,1,\ldots,A\}.
\]
For $m\ge 1$, set
\[
X_m^{(A)}
:=
\{x\in \mathcal A_A^m:\ x_k=A\Rightarrow x_{k-1}=0
\text{ for }2\le k\le m\},
\]
and define
\[
\Rank_{A,m}(x):=\sum_{k=1}^m x_k Q_{k-1}^{(A)}.
\]
The corresponding cyclic rank recoding is
\[
\Fold_{A,m}(\omega)
:=
\bigl(\Rank_{A,m}|_{X_m^{(A)}}\bigr)^{-1}
\bigl(\Rank_{A,m}(\omega)\bmod Q_m^{(A)}\bigr),
\]
whenever the displayed restriction is bijective. For $m\ge2$, define the
sliding stabilized-window map and its image by
\[
(\Phi_{A,m}(a))_t:=\Fold_{A,m}(a_t,\ldots,a_{t+m-1}),
\qquad
Y_{A,m}:=\Phi_{A,m}(\mathcal A_A^{\mathbb Z}).
\]
For $n\ge1$, the corresponding finite-block map is
\[
\Phi_{A,m,n}:\mathcal A_A^{n+m-1}\longrightarrow (X_m^{(A)})^n,
\qquad
\Phi_{A,m,n}(a_0\ldots a_{n+m-2})
:=\bigl(\Fold_{A,m}(a_t,\ldots,a_{t+m-1})\bigr)_{t=0}^{n-1}.
\]
The notation $\Phi_{A,2}$ and $Y_{A,2}$ is the specialization $m=2$.
\end{definition}

The bijectivity clause in Definition~\ref{def:metallic-window-data} holds for
every $A\ge1$ and $m\ge1$: for $A=1$ it is
Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-window-range}, via
Lemma~\ref{lem:metallic-golden-member} below, and for $A\ge2$ it is proved in
Theorem~\ref{thm:metallic-two-window-rigidity}(i).

\begin{definition}[Nontrivial metallic conjugacy threshold]
\label{def:metallic-conjugacy-threshold}
For $A\ge1$, define
\[
m_*(\beta_A):=\min\{m\ge2:\Phi_{A,m}\text{ is a topological conjugacy
onto the SFT }Y_{A,m}\}.
\]
The restriction $m\ge2$ is essential: at $m=1$ the legal alphabet is all of
$\mathcal A_A$, the modulus is $Q_1^{(A)}=A+1$, and $\Fold_{A,1}$ is the
identity.  Including this trivial aperture would therefore obscure the
golden failure at $m=2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[Scope of the beta-family statement]
\label{rem:metallic-beta-scope}
In this section, ``metallic quadratic Pisot base'' means precisely
$\beta_A$, the positive root of $x^2-Ax-1$, with integer $A\ge1$, together
with the digit set, admissibility rule, language rank and cyclic modulus in
Definition~\ref{def:metallic-window-data}.  The extension to other quadratic
minimal polynomials uses the distinct canonical rank construction of
Definition~\ref{def:quadratic-parry-fold} and is proved in
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold}.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Boundary-modified constant-type recurrence model]
\label{lem:constant-type-ostrowski-origin}
Let
\[
\alpha_A=[0;A,A,A,\ldots],\qquad A\ge1,
\]
and let $(q_n)$ be the denominators of its continued-fraction convergents, with
$q_{-1}=0$ and $q_0=1$. Then
\[
q_{n+1}=Aq_n+q_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge0).
\]
With the finite-window indexing
\[
Q_j^{(A)}:=q_j+q_{j-1}\qquad(j\ge0),
\]
this is exactly
\[
Q_0^{(A)}=1,\qquad Q_1^{(A)}=A+1,\qquad
Q_{j+2}^{(A)}=AQ_{j+1}^{(A)}+Q_j^{(A)}.
\]
The local constraint used in Definition~\ref{def:metallic-window-data} is the
constant-type Ostrowski constraint
\[
x_k\in\{0,\ldots,A\},\qquad x_k=A\Rightarrow x_{k-1}=0 .
\]
However, the model is not the standard Ostrowski representation associated
with $\alpha_A$: standard digits are weighted by $q_j$, and the first digit
has the additional boundary restriction determined by the first partial
quotient.  Here the weights are $Q_j^{(A)}=q_j+q_{j-1}$ and the lowest digit
$x_1=A$ is permitted.  It is therefore a boundary-modified constant-type
recurrence model using the Ostrowski local constraint, followed by cyclic
language-rank reduction.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a continued fraction $[0;a_1,a_2,\ldots]$, the denominator recurrence is
\[
q_{n+1}=a_{n+1}q_n+q_{n-1},
\qquad q_{-1}=0,\quad q_0=1 .
\]
Since every partial quotient here is $A$, the displayed recurrence follows.
The sequence
$Q_j^{(A)}=q_j+q_{j-1}$ has $Q_0^{(A)}=1$ and $Q_1^{(A)}=A+1$, and it satisfies
the same constant recurrence by linearity:
\[
Q_{j+2}^{(A)}
=q_{j+2}+q_{j+1}
=A(q_{j+1}+q_j)+(q_j+q_{j-1})
=AQ_{j+1}^{(A)}+Q_j^{(A)}.
\]
Thus the modulus obeys the usual constant-type denominator recurrence but has
the boundary modification $Q_j^{(A)}=q_j+q_{j-1}$, analogous to using
$F_{m+2}$ in the golden finite-window model.

Away from the lowest digit, the Ostrowski admissibility rule for constant
partial quotients is $0\le x_k\le A$ and, whenever $x_k=A$, the preceding
lower digit is zero.  This is the local greedy uniqueness condition: if
$x_k=A$ and $x_{k-1}>0$, then the recurrence permits a carry replacing
$Aq_k+x_{k-1}q_{k-1}$ by $q_{k+1}+(x_{k-1}-1)q_{k-1}$, so the expansion is not
greedy; conversely the greedy algorithm never creates the forbidden adjacent
pattern.  Definition~\ref{def:metallic-window-data} deliberately retains this
local rule while changing both the weights and the lower boundary.  Standard
Ostrowski conventions and their first-digit restriction are described in
\cite{HieronymiTerry2018}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Golden member of the metallic notation]\label{lem:metallic-golden-member}
If the formulas of Definition~\ref{def:metallic-window-data} are evaluated at
$A=1$, then
\[
Q_j^{(1)}=F_{j+2},\qquad
X_m^{(1)}=X_m,\qquad
\Rank_{1,m}=\Val_m,\qquad
\Fold_{1,m}=\Fold_m.
\]
In particular $\Phi_{1,2}$ is exactly the Fibonacci two-window map $\Phi_2$.
Together with Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-type-ostrowski-origin}, this identifies
the golden case as the formal $A=1$ endpoint of the same self-contained
boundary-modified constant-type recurrence model; no identification with a
standard Ostrowski representation is used in the comparison theorem.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The sequence $(Q_j^{(1)})$ has initial values $Q_0^{(1)}=1=F_2$ and
$Q_1^{(1)}=2=F_3$, and satisfies
$Q_{j+2}^{(1)}=Q_{j+1}^{(1)}+Q_j^{(1)}$.  Hence
$Q_j^{(1)}=F_{j+2}$ for all $j$.

When $A=1$, the alphabet is $\{0,1\}$ and the legality condition
$x_k=1\Rightarrow x_{k-1}=0$ is exactly the no-adjacent-ones condition
defining $X_m$.  The language-rank formula becomes
\[
\Rank_{1,m}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^m x_kQ_{k-1}^{(1)}
=\sum_{k=1}^m x_kF_{k+1}=\Val_m(x).
\]
The modulus $Q_m^{(1)}$ is $F_{m+2}$, so the two definitions of finite-window
cyclic rank recoding agree.  Applying this at every coordinate for $m=2$ gives
$\Phi_{1,2}=\Phi_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-window rigidity]
\label{thm:metallic-two-window-rigidity}
Within the boundary-modified constant-type cyclic rank family of
Definition~\ref{def:metallic-window-data}, for every integer $A\ge 2$ the
following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
  \item For every $m\ge 1$, the restriction
  \[
  \Rank_{A,m}|_{X_m^{(A)}}:X_m^{(A)}\to
  \{0,1,\ldots,Q_m^{(A)}-1\}
  \]
  is a bijection.
  \item At $m=2$ the cyclic rank recoding is explicit:
  \[
  \Fold_{A,2}(u,v)=
  \begin{cases}
  (u,v), & v<A\text{ or }u=0,\\
  (u-1,0), & v=A\text{ and }u\ge 1.
  \end{cases}
  \]
  \item The two-window sliding map
  \[
  \Phi_{A,2}:(\mathcal A_A^{\mathbb Z},\sigma)\to
  (Y_{A,2},\sigma),
  \qquad
  Y_{A,2}:=\Phi_{A,2}(\mathcal A_A^{\mathbb Z}),
  \]
  is a topological conjugacy onto its image.  Its inverse is the
  two-symbol sliding-block code
  \[
  a_t=\psi_A(y_{t-1},y_t),\qquad y=\Phi_{A,2}(a),
  \]
  where, for $y_s=(p_s,q_s)\in X_2^{(A)}$,
  \[
  \psi_A(y_{t-1},y_t)=
  \begin{cases}
  q_{t-1}, & q_{t-1}>0,\\
  0, & q_{t-1}=0\text{ and }p_t=0,\\
  A, & q_{t-1}=0\text{ and }p_t\in\{A-1,A\}.
  \end{cases}
  \]
  The three alternatives are exhaustive for pairs in $\mathcal L_2(Y_{A,2})$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, within the boundary-modified constant-type cyclic rank family
of Definition~\ref{def:metallic-window-data}, the golden case $A=1$ is
the only member of this model in which a nontrivial two-window branch locus
remains.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First prove the finite-window range statement.  Let $N_m:=|X_m^{(A)}|$.
Clearly $N_0=1$ and $N_1=A+1$.  For $m\ge2$, a legal word ending in a digit
$0,\ldots,A-1$ has an arbitrary legal prefix of length $m-1$, while a legal
word ending in $A$ must have penultimate digit $0$ and therefore has an
arbitrary legal prefix of length $m-2$.  Hence
\[
N_m=A N_{m-1}+N_{m-2}.
\]
Thus $N_m=Q_m^{(A)}$ for all $m$.

The same last-digit decomposition proves that the rank gives disjoint
consecutive intervals. For $m=1$ this is immediate. Assume the statement
known up to length $m-1$. If the last digit is $d<A$, then
\[
\Rank_{A,m}(x)=\Rank_{A,m-1}(x_1,\ldots,x_{m-1})+dQ_{m-1}^{(A)}
\]
runs through the interval
\[
[dQ_{m-1}^{(A)},(d+1)Q_{m-1}^{(A)}-1].
\]
As $d=0,\ldots,A-1$, these intervals cover
$[0,AQ_{m-1}^{(A)}-1]$. If the last digit is $A$, legality forces
$x_{m-1}=0$, and the remaining prefix of length $m-2$ gives precisely
\[
[AQ_{m-1}^{(A)},AQ_{m-1}^{(A)}+Q_{m-2}^{(A)}-1]
=[AQ_{m-1}^{(A)},Q_m^{(A)}-1].
\]
The intervals are disjoint and cover exactly
$\{0,\ldots,Q_m^{(A)}-1\}$.  This proves (i).

For $m=2$ one has $Q_2^{(A)}=A^2+A+1$ and
\[
\Rank_{A,2}(u,v)=u+(A+1)v.
\]
If $v<A$ or $u=0$, the pair $(u,v)$ is legal and its rank lies in
$[0,Q_2^{(A)}-1]$, so it is fixed by the recoding.  If $v=A$ and $u\ge1$,
then
\[
u+(A+1)A=Q_2^{(A)}+(u-1),
\]
whose residue is $u-1$.  The unique legal pair of rank $u-1$ is
$(u-1,0)$.  This proves (ii).

It remains to prove the path-space assertion. Let
$a\in\mathcal A_A^{\mathbb Z}$ and $y=\Phi_{A,2}(a)$, with
$y_t=(p_t,q_t)$.  By the explicit formula in (ii), if $q_{t-1}>0$ then the
raw second digit of the pair $(a_{t-1},a_t)$ is exactly $q_{t-1}$, hence
$a_t=q_{t-1}$.

Suppose next that $q_{t-1}=0$.  The explicit formula in (ii) shows that the
only possible values of $a_t$ are $0$ and $A$.  If $a_t=0$, then the next raw
pair starts with $0$, is already legal for every value of $a_{t+1}$, and its
recoded output has first coordinate $p_t=0$.  If $a_t=A$, then the next raw
pair starts with $A$.  When $a_{t+1}<A$, the pair is legal and the next output
has first coordinate $p_t=A$; when $a_{t+1}=A$, the pair $(A,A)$ is recoded to
$(A-1,0)$ and the next output has first coordinate $p_t=A-1$.  Since
$A\ge2$, the sets $\{0\}$ and $\{A-1,A\}$ are disjoint.  Therefore the displayed
formula for $\psi_A$ recovers $a_t$ uniquely from $(y_{t-1},y_t)$.

The map $\Phi_{A,2}$ is continuous, shift-equivariant and surjective onto
$Y_{A,2}$ by definition. The preceding local formula gives a continuous
shift-equivariant inverse on $Y_{A,2}$, proving that $\Phi_{A,2}$ is a
topological conjugacy onto its image.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:metallic-golden-member}, the formal $A=1$ member of this
notation is the Fibonacci map $\Phi_2$.  For $A=1$, the separating sets become
$\{0\}$ and $\{0,1\}$, so the preceding local distinction collapses. The
remaining ambiguity is exactly the golden two-window branch locus classified
in Theorem~\ref{thm:m2-branch-locus}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The family-wide block threshold and conjugacy}

\begin{theorem}[Metallic family block-bijection theorem]
\label{thm:metallic-family-block-bijection}
Let $A\ge1$ be an integer, let $m\ge2$, and assume
\[
(A,m)\ne(1,2).
\]
Then, for every $n\ge m$, the finite-block map
\[
\Phi_{A,m,n}:\mathcal A_A^{n+m-1}\longrightarrow (X_m^{(A)})^n
\]
is injective.  Equivalently, it is a bijection from its domain onto the
length-$n$ language of $Y_{A,m}$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:metallic-block-count}
|\mathcal L_n(Y_{A,m})|=(A+1)^{n+m-1}\qquad(n\ge m).
\end{equation}
For $A=1$, this is the Fibonacci block-bijection theorem
Theorem~\ref{thm:block-invertibility}; in particular it retains its explicit
three-window decoder from Lemma~\ref{lem:m3-decoder}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The specialization $A=1$ is exactly
Theorem~\ref{thm:block-invertibility}, in view of
Lemma~\ref{lem:metallic-golden-member}.  We therefore assume $A\ge2$.
Write $Q_j=Q_j^{(A)}$ for brevity.  Since
Theorem~\ref{thm:metallic-two-window-rigidity}(i) makes
$\Rank_{A,m}|_{X_m^{(A)}}$ bijective, equality of stabilized output words is
equivalent to equality of their language-rank residues modulo $Q_m$.

We first prove injectivity for $n=m$, treating the two small apertures
separately.

Suppose $m=2$.  A raw block $a_0a_1a_2$ produces two outputs
$y_0,y_1$.  The local rule in
Theorem~\ref{thm:metallic-two-window-rigidity}(iii), applied with $t=1$,
recovers $a_1$ from $(y_0,y_1)$.  If
\[
r_i:=\Rank_{A,2}(y_i),\qquad i=0,1,
\]
then
\[
r_0\equiv a_0+Q_1a_1,\qquad
r_1\equiv a_1+Q_1a_2\pmod {Q_2}.
\]
The first congruence recovers $a_0$, because two candidates differ by an
integer of modulus at most $A<Q_2$.  The second recovers $a_2$: indeed
$\gcd(Q_1,Q_2)=\gcd(A+1,A^2+A+1)=1$, so equality for two candidates would
imply that $Q_2$ divides their difference, whose modulus is at most $A$.
Thus $\Phi_{A,2,2}$ is injective.

Suppose next that $m=3$.  Let $a_0\ldots a_4$ and $b_0\ldots b_4$ have the
same three output residues, and put
\[
d_i:=a_i-b_i\in[-A,A].
\]
Using $Q_0=1$, $Q_1=A+1$ and
$Q_{j+2}=AQ_{j+1}+Q_j$, the combination of the three residue congruences
with coefficients $1,-A,-1$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:metallic-m3-difference}
d_0+d_1-Q_2d_4\equiv0\pmod {Q_3}.
\end{equation}
Set $s=d_0+d_1$, so $|s|\le2A$.  Since
\[
Q_2=A^2+A+1>2A,\qquad Q_3=AQ_2+Q_1,
\]
the distance of $dQ_2$ from $Q_3\ZZ$ is greater than $2A$ whenever
$1\le |d|\le A-1$.  For $d=A$ one has
$AQ_2=Q_3-Q_1$, and the case $d=-A$ is symmetric.  Hence
\eqref{eq:metallic-m3-difference} leaves precisely the alternatives
\[
(d_4,s)=(0,0),\qquad (A,-Q_1),\qquad(-A,Q_1).
\]

If $d_4=0$, equality of the last output residue gives
\[
d_2+Q_1d_3\equiv0\pmod {Q_3}.
\]
Its left-hand side has modulus at most $A+AQ_1=A^2+2A<Q_3$, so it is zero
as an integer.  Since $|d_2|\le A<Q_1$, this forces $d_2=d_3=0$.  The first
residue then similarly gives $d_0+Q_1d_1=0$, whence $d_0=d_1=0$.

If $d_4=A$, the last residue congruence and
$AQ_2=Q_3-Q_1$ give
\[
d_2+Q_1(d_3-1)\equiv0\pmod {Q_3}.
\]
The modulus of the left-hand side is at most
$A+Q_1(A+1)=A^2+3A+1<Q_3$, where the last inequality is
$A^3-A>0$.  Thus it is zero as an integer, and
$|d_2|<Q_1$ forces $(d_2,d_3)=(0,1)$.  The middle residue congruence would
then be
\[
d_1+Q_2\equiv0\pmod {Q_3},
\]
which is impossible because
$0<Q_2-A\le d_1+Q_2\le Q_2+A<Q_3$.  The case $d_4=-A$ is symmetric: it
forces $(d_2,d_3)=(0,-1)$ and then the nonzero integer $d_1-Q_2$, of modulus
less than $Q_3$, would be divisible by $Q_3$.  Therefore all $d_i$ vanish,
and $\Phi_{A,3,3}$ is injective.

Now let $m\ge4$.  Suppose two raw blocks
$a_0\ldots a_{2m-2}$ and $b_0\ldots b_{2m-2}$ have the same $m$ output
residues, and again put $d_i=a_i-b_i$.  For $0\le t\le m-3$, take the
linear combination with coefficients $1,-A,-1$ of the residue congruences
at $t,t+1,t+2$.  All interior coefficients cancel by the recurrence, the
coefficient at $d_{t+m}$ is $-AQ_{m-1}-Q_{m-2}=-Q_m$, and the final
coefficient is $-Q_{m-1}$.  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:metallic-large-m-difference}
d_t+d_{t+1}-Q_{m-1}d_{t+m+1}\equiv0\pmod {Q_m}.
\end{equation}
We claim that this forces $d_{t+m+1}=0$.  Indeed,
\[
Q_{m-2}\ge Q_2=A^2+A+1>2A.
\]
For $1\le d\le A$, the number $dQ_{m-1}$ lies strictly between $0$ and
$Q_m=AQ_{m-1}+Q_{m-2}$, and its distances from the two endpoints satisfy
\[
dQ_{m-1}\ge Q_{m-1}>2A,
\]
\[
Q_m-dQ_{m-1}=(A-d)Q_{m-1}+Q_{m-2}>2A.
\]
The same holds for negative $d$ by symmetry.  Since
$|d_t+d_{t+1}|\le2A$, congruence
\eqref{eq:metallic-large-m-difference} is therefore possible only when
$d_{t+m+1}=0$; it then also gives $d_t+d_{t+1}=0$.  Varying $t$ yields
\[
d_{m+1}=d_{m+2}=\cdots=d_{2m-2}=0.
\]

The last output-residue congruence now reduces to
\[
d_{m-1}+Q_1d_m\equiv0\pmod {Q_m}.
\]
Its left-hand side has modulus at most $A+AQ_1=A^2+2A<Q_m$, so it vanishes
as an integer.  Because $Q_1=A+1>|d_{m-1}|$, this forces
$d_{m-1}=d_m=0$.  Moving backwards through the residue congruences, at
stage $j=m-2,m-3,\ldots,0$ every term except $d_jQ_0=d_j$ is already zero.
Thus $d_j\equiv0\pmod {Q_m}$, and $|d_j|\le A<Q_m$ gives $d_j=0$.  This
proves injectivity of $\Phi_{A,m,m}$ for every $m\ge4$.

Finally let $n\ge m$.  If two raw blocks have the same length-$n$ output,
then every consecutive length-$m$ output subblock is equal.  The established
injectivity of $\Phi_{A,m,m}$ makes the corresponding raw subblocks of length
$2m-1$ equal.  These subblocks cover all $n+m-1$ raw coordinates, so the raw
blocks are equal.  Every raw finite block extends to a bi-infinite element of
the full shift $\mathcal A_A^{\ZZ}$; hence the image of
$\Phi_{A,m,n}$ is exactly $\mathcal L_n(Y_{A,m})$.  Counting the domain gives
\eqref{eq:metallic-block-count}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp metallic threshold classification]
\label{thm:metallic-threshold-classification}
Let $A\ge1$ be an integer and let
$\beta_A=(A+\sqrt{A^2+4})/2$.  Use exactly the alphabet, legal language,
rank, modulus and fold of Definition~\ref{def:metallic-window-data}, and
exclude the trivial aperture $m=1$ as in
Definition~\ref{def:metallic-conjugacy-threshold}.  Then
\[
\{m\ge2:\Phi_{A,m}\text{ is a topological conjugacy onto the SFT }
Y_{A,m}\}
=
\begin{cases}
\{3,4,5,\ldots\},&A=1,\\
\{2,3,4,\ldots\},&A\ge2.
\end{cases}
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:metallic-threshold-function}
m_*(\beta_A)=
\begin{cases}
3,&A=1,\\
2,&A\ge2.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
In particular, the golden mean
$\beta_1=(1+\sqrt5)/2$ is the unique metallic quadratic Pisot base with
$m_*(\beta_A)=3$.  At every aperture in the displayed conjugacy set, the
inverse is a sliding-block code with memory $0$ and anticipation $m-1$, and
$Y_{A,m}$ is defined by finitely many forbidden words of length at most
$m+1$ over $X_m^{(A)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix $(A,m)\ne(1,2)$ with $A\ge1$ and $m\ge2$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:metallic-family-block-bijection} says that every word
$W\in\mathcal L_m(Y_{A,m})$ has a unique raw preimage
\[
\Psi_{A,m,m}(W)\in\mathcal A_A^{2m-1}.
\]
Let $\psi_{A,m}(W)$ be the first symbol of this raw block.  If
$y=\Phi_{A,m}(a)$, then the output block
$(y_t,\ldots,y_{t+m-1})$ is the image of
$a_t\ldots a_{t+2m-2}$, so uniqueness gives
\[
a_t=\psi_{A,m}(y_t,\ldots,y_{t+m-1}).
\]
This is a memory-$0$, anticipation-$(m-1)$ continuous shift-commuting inverse
on $Y_{A,m}$.  Since $Y_{A,m}$ is the image by definition, it is a two-sided
inverse and $\Phi_{A,m}$ is a topological conjugacy.

For completeness, the image is of finite type by the same decoded-block
criterion.  A sequence $y\in(X_m^{(A)})^{\ZZ}$ belongs to $Y_{A,m}$ if and
only if every length-$m$ word
$W_t=(y_t,\ldots,y_{t+m-1})$ lies in $\mathcal L_m(Y_{A,m})$ and
\[
\Psi_{A,m,m}(W_t)_{1,\ldots,2m-2}
=\Psi_{A,m,m}(W_{t+1})_{0,\ldots,2m-3}
\quad(t\in\ZZ).
\]
Necessity follows from overlapping raw windows.  Conversely, these equalities
glue the decoded blocks into a unique $a\in\mathcal A_A^{\ZZ}$ and applying
$\Phi_{A,m,m}$ to each glued block gives $y=\Phi_{A,m}(a)$.  The criterion
depends only on output words of length $m+1$, so finitely many such words form
a forbidden list.

It remains only to identify the excluded pair.  When $A=1$, the data is
Fibonacci by Lemma~\ref{lem:metallic-golden-member}, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:m2-branch-locus} gives
\[
\Phi_{1,2}^{-1}((\ldots,00,00,\ldots))=\{0^{\ZZ},1^{\ZZ}\}.
\]
Thus $\Phi_{1,2}$ is not injective.  Every other pair $(A,m)$ is conjugate by
the preceding argument.  The two alternatives exhaust all $A\ge1$ and
$m\ge2$, proving the conjugacy sets, the threshold formula, and golden
uniqueness.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Entropy and dynamical-zeta certificate for golden extremality]
\label{thm:metallic-entropy-zeta-extremality}
Under the hypotheses and notation of
Theorem~\ref{thm:metallic-threshold-classification}, for every $m\ge2$,
\[
h_{\rm top}(Y_{A,m})=\log(A+1).
\]
For every $n\ge1$, the periodic-point counts and Artin--Mazur zeta functions
are
\[
\#\operatorname{Fix}(\sigma^n|_{Y_{A,m}})
=
\begin{cases}
2^n-1,&(A,m)=(1,2),\\
(A+1)^n,&(A,m)\ne(1,2),
\end{cases}
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:metallic-zeta-classification}
\zeta_{Y_{A,m}}(z)
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1-z}{1-2z},&(A,m)=(1,2),\\[6pt]
\dfrac{1}{1-(A+1)z},&(A,m)\ne(1,2).
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
In particular, the entropy-normalized two-window zeta defect
\[
\mathcal D_A(z):=(1-(A+1)z)\zeta_{Y_{A,2}}(z)
\]
satisfies
\[
\mathcal D_A(z)=
\begin{cases}
1-z,&A=1,\\
1,&A\ge2.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus entropy records the full-shift exponential growth but does not see the
golden two-window branch, whereas the zeta numerator detects exactly the
unique parameter with $m_*(\beta_A)=3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $(A,m)\ne(1,2)$, Theorem~\ref{thm:metallic-threshold-classification}
gives a topological conjugacy with the full shift on $A+1$ symbols.  Entropy,
periodic-point counts and the Artin--Mazur zeta function are conjugacy
invariants, so in this case they are
\[
\log(A+1),\qquad (A+1)^n,\qquad
\exp\left(\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(A+1)^nz^n}{n}\right)
=\frac1{1-(A+1)z}.
\]

Consider $(A,m)=(1,2)$.  Let $\mathbf0$ denote the constant output point
$(\ldots,00,00,\ldots)$.  If $y\in Y_{1,2}$ satisfies $\sigma^ny=y$ and
$y\ne\mathbf0$, choose a lift $a$.  Then
\[
\Phi_{1,2}(\sigma^na)=\sigma^ny=y=\Phi_{1,2}(a).
\]
Theorem~\ref{thm:m2-branch-locus} says that the fiber of $y$ is a singleton,
so $\sigma^na=a$.  The fiber of $\mathbf0$ consists exactly of the two fixed
points $0^{\ZZ}$ and $1^{\ZZ}$.  Hence the map from the $2^n$ points fixed by
$\sigma^n$ in the full two-shift onto
$\operatorname{Fix}(\sigma^n|_{Y_{1,2}})$ identifies precisely these two
constant points and nothing else.  Therefore the image has $2^n-1$ fixed
points.  It follows that
\[
\zeta_{Y_{1,2}}(z)
=\exp\left(\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(2^n-1)z^n}{n}\right)
=\frac{1-z}{1-2z}.
\]
The factor inequality gives $h_{\rm top}(Y_{1,2})\le\log2$, while the
$2^n-1$ distinct $n$-periodic points give
\[
h_{\rm top}(Y_{1,2})\ge
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log(2^n-1)=\log2.
\]
This proves the entropy identity in the remaining case.  Multiplication of
the two-window zeta formulas by $1-(A+1)z$ gives the stated defect.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The Fibonacci image as a Fischer cover}

The overlap graph $\mathcal G_m$ gives a concrete presentation of $Y_m$. Above
threshold it is the canonical minimal right-resolving presentation of $Y_m$
in the stabilized output alphabet.

We use the following standard characterization of the right Fischer cover of
an irreducible synchronized sofic shift: the right Fischer cover is the
canonical right-resolving graph whose vertices are the follower sets of
intrinsically synchronizing words, with transitions
\[
F_X(w)\xrightarrow{a}F_X(wa)
\quad\text{whenever }wa\in\mathcal L(X).
\]
It is follower-separated and is minimal among essential irreducible
right-resolving presentations. This is the Fischer--Krieger cover
construction in its right-resolving form; see
\cite{Fischer1975,Krieger1984,Krieger1987,LindMarcus1995,Kitchens1998,BoyleKitchensMarcus1985,Johansen2011}.
The lemma below is the concrete criterion needed for the overlap graph.

For a vertex $u\in V_m=\{0,1\}^{m-1}$, let
\[
\mathcal F^+(u):=
\{w\in X_m^*:\text{ there exists a path in }\mathcal G_m
\text{ beginning at }u\text{ with label }w\}
\]
be its right follower language.

\begin{lemma}[Fischer-cover criterion]\label{lem:fischer-cover-criterion}
Let $X$ be an irreducible sofic shift and let $G$ be an essential irreducible
right-resolving presentation of $X$. Assume in addition that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
  \item $G$ is follower-separated, meaning distinct vertices have distinct
  right follower languages in $X$;
  \item every vertex $v$ of $G$ is the terminal vertex of a path whose label
  $w_v$ is intrinsically synchronizing for $X$ and labels a unique path in
  $G$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $G$ is the right Fischer cover of $X$. In particular, every essential
irreducible right-resolving presentation of $X$ has at least as many vertices
as $G$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
This is the standard Fischer-cover theorem for irreducible sofic shifts:
among essential irreducible right-resolving presentations, the unique
follower-separated presentation in which each state is reached by an
intrinsically synchronizing word is the right Fischer cover; equivalently it
is the canonical graph of synchronizing follower sets. See
\cite[Theorem~3.3.18]{LindMarcus1995} and the Fischer--Krieger cover
references cited above.

The unique-path clause in (ii) identifies the terminal vertex reached by
$w_v$ with the canonical follower-set vertex $F_X(w_v)$, while
follower-separatedness prevents two vertices of $G$ from representing the
same follower set. Right-resolvingness gives the canonical transition rule on
these follower sets. Hence the standard theorem identifies $G$ with the right
Fischer cover. Its minimality among essential irreducible right-resolving
presentations gives the stated state lower bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Fischer cover of the stabilized image]
\label{thm:fischer-cover-stabilized-image}
Assume $m\ge3$.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
  \item Every word $w\in\mathcal L_m(Y_m)$ labels exactly one path of length
  $m$ in the overlap graph $\mathcal G_m$. Consequently every word in
  $\mathcal L_m(Y_m)$ is intrinsically synchronizing for $Y_m$.
  \item The follower languages $\mathcal F^+(u)$, $u\in V_m$, are pairwise
  distinct.  Hence $\mathcal G_m$ is follower-separated.
  \item The labeled graph $\mathcal G_m$ is the right Fischer cover of $Y_m$.
  In particular, every essential irreducible right-resolving presentation of
  $Y_m$ has at least $2^{m-1}$ vertices.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A path of length $m$ in $\mathcal G_m$ is exactly a raw binary block
\[
b_0b_1\cdots b_{2m-2}\in\{0,1\}^{2m-1},
\]
and its label is
\[
\Phi_{m,m}(b_0b_1\cdots b_{2m-2}).
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:block-invertibility}, the map $\Phi_{m,m}$ is injective.
Thus each legal word $w\in\mathcal L_m(Y_m)$ has a unique preimage raw
block and hence labels exactly one path in $\mathcal G_m$.

The same uniqueness gives intrinsic synchronization. If $uw$ and $wv$ are
admissible words in $Y_m$, then in any path labeled by $uw$ the subpath labeled
by $w$ is the unique path labeled by $w$, and similarly for any path labeled by
$wv$.  The first path therefore reaches the terminal vertex of this unique
$w$-path, and the second path leaves that same terminal vertex after reading
$w$.  Concatenation gives an admissible path labeled by $uwv$.  Hence $w$ is
intrinsically synchronizing.  This proves (i).

Let $u,v\in V_m$ with $u\ne v$.  Choose any path of length $m$ beginning at
$u$, and let $w$ be its label.  If $w$ also belonged to $\mathcal F^+(v)$, then
$w$ would label a second length-$m$ path, now beginning at $v$.  This contradicts
(i), since the initial vertices are different.  Thus
$\mathcal F^+(u)\ne\mathcal F^+(v)$, proving (ii).

It remains to verify the hypotheses of
Lemma~\ref{lem:fischer-cover-criterion}. The graph $\mathcal G_m$ is finite by
definition. The underlying de Bruijn graph on
$\{0,1\}^{m-1}$ is essential: every vertex
$u=(u_1,\ldots,u_{m-1})$ lies on a bi-infinite path, obtained for example by
using the periodic raw sequence with period $u$ when $u$ is nonempty. It is
irreducible because, from any vertex $u$ to any vertex $v$, one follows the
raw word obtained by appending the symbols of $v$ after $u$, which gives a
path whose terminal vertex is $v$. Hence the presented shift $Y_m$ is
irreducible and $\mathcal G_m$ is an essential irreducible presentation.
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-state-lift} proves that the labeling is
right-resolving, so $\mathcal G_m$ is an essential irreducible
right-resolving presentation of $Y_m$. Statement (ii) above proves the
additional follower-separation hypothesis.

Finally, every vertex is the terminal vertex of some length-$m$ path: append
the symbols of that vertex after any initial bit. By (i), the label of every
length-$m$ path labels a unique path and is intrinsically synchronizing. Thus
every vertex is reached by a unique-path intrinsically synchronizing word,
verifying the remaining synchronizing-word hypothesis.
Lemma~\ref{lem:fischer-cover-criterion} therefore identifies $\mathcal G_m$
with the right Fischer cover of $Y_m$ and gives the lower bound for all
essential irreducible right-resolving presentations. The vertex set has
cardinality $|V_m|=2^{m-1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Alphabet dependence of the state count]
The $2^{m-1}$ states are forced among essential irreducible right-resolving
presentations of the particular labeled shift $Y_m\subset X_m^{\mathbb Z}$.
This is not a conjugacy-invariant complexity measure.  Indeed
Theorem~\ref{thm:two-sided-conjugacy} conjugates $Y_m$ to the binary full
shift, whose usual Fischer cover has one state.  The state conclusion is
therefore canonical relative to the stabilized output alphabet and its
language, not under arbitrary recoding of the dynamical system.
\end{remark}

\section{Cyclic rank recoding for quadratic Pisot languages}
\label{sec:quadratic-pisot-extension}

This section closes the interface left by Remark~\ref{rem:metallic-beta-scope}.
The point requiring care is that a quadratic Pisot number need not be a unit
and its conjugate need not be negative.  Consequently the boundary-modified
constant-type language is not the appropriate common object.  We instead use
the greedy $\beta$-language and its colexicographic ordered-language rank, and
we introduce a cyclic reduction of that rank.  This recoding is not numerical
$\beta$-value normalization: it asserts congruence only between integer
language ranks and does not assert equality in $\mathbb Z[\beta]$.  The
classical $\beta$-shift and automata literature supplies context
\cite{Renyi1957,ItoTakahashi1974,Parry1960,Blanchard1989,Loraud1995,
BruyereHansel1997,LecomteRigo2001}; every finite-rank and
sliding-congruence statement used below is proved here.

\subsection{Quadratic classification and canonical finite windows}

\begin{lemma}[The two quadratic Pisot parameter chambers]
\label{lem:quadratic-pisot-chambers}
Let $\beta>1$ be a quadratic algebraic integer and let $\beta'$ be its
conjugate.  Then $|\beta'|<1$ if and only if the minimal polynomial of
$\beta$ belongs to exactly one of the following two families:
\begin{align*}
P^-_{a,b}(x)&=x^2-ax-b, & a\ge b\ge1,\\
P^+_{a,b}(x)&=x^2-ax+b, & a\ge3,\quad 1\le b\le a-2.
\end{align*}
In the first chamber $\beta'<0$, $\lfloor\beta\rfloor=a$, and
\[
d_\beta(1)=ab0^\infty,\qquad
d_\beta^*(1)=\bigl(a(b-1)\bigr)^\infty.
\]
In the second chamber $\beta'>0$, $\lfloor\beta\rfloor=a-1$, and
\[
d_\beta(1)=(a-1)(a-b-1)^\infty=d_\beta^*(1).
\]
Here $d_\beta$ is the greedy expansion and $d_\beta^*$ is Parry's
quasi-greedy boundary word.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write the monic minimal polynomial as $x^2-ax+c$.  Since
$c=\beta\beta'\ne0$, the sign of $c$ is the sign of $\beta'$.  If
$c=-b<0$, then $b/\beta=|\beta'|<1$.  The positive root exceeds $a$;
the last inequality is equivalent, for integral $a,b$, to $1\le b\le a$.
Conversely these inequalities place the negative root in $(-1,0)$.
If $c=b>0$, then $0<b/\beta=\beta'<1$ and $a-1<\beta<a$; evaluating
$P^+_{a,b}$ at $a-1$ and $a$ gives exactly $a\ge3$ and
$1\le b\le a-2$.  The converses follow from the same sign test.

For $P^-_{a,b}$ one has $\beta^2=a\beta+b$.  The greedy algorithm applied
to $1$ therefore gives the two digits $a,b$ and then terminates; Parry's
standard replacement of a finite expansion gives
$d_\beta^*(1)=(a(b-1))^\infty$.  For $P^+_{a,b}$, put
$r=\beta-a+1=1-b/\beta$.  Then
$\lfloor\beta\rfloor=a-1$ and
\[
\beta r=\beta-b=(a-b-1)+r,
\]
so every digit after the first is $a-b-1$.  The expansion is infinite and
hence already quasi-greedy.  This is precisely Parry's calculation
\cite{Parry1960}; it is included to fix the parameters, not as a new proof of
his general admissibility theorem.
\end{proof}

For either chamber put $d=\lfloor\beta\rfloor$ and
$\mathcal A_\beta=\{0,\ldots,d\}$.  Let $\mathcal L_m(X_\beta)$ be the
length-$m$ language of the two-sided greedy $\beta$-shift, characterized by
Parry's suffix inequalities against $d_\beta^*(1)$.

For words $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)$ and $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)$ in low-to-high
orientation, write $x<_{\rm colex}y$ when
$(x_m,\ldots,x_1)<_{\rm lex}(y_m,\ldots,y_1)$.  Lexicographic comparison of a
finite word with an infinite boundary uses the available finite prefix: the
first unequal digit decides the comparison, and equality through the end of
the finite word is allowed.  A comparison with $c_0^m$ is the literal
finite-word comparison.

\begin{definition}[Cyclic rank recoding attached to the Parry language]
\label{def:quadratic-parry-fold}
For $m\ge0$ define $Q_m(\beta)=|\mathcal L_m(X_\beta)|$; the recurrences for
these counts are proved in Proposition~\ref{prop:parry-rank-bijection}.
Use the low-to-high orientation
\[
X_m^{(\beta)}:=\{x\in\mathcal A_\beta^m:
(x_m,\ldots,x_1)\in\mathcal L_m(X_\beta)\}
\]
and set
\[
\operatorname{Rank}_{\beta,m}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}x_{j+1}Q_j(\beta).
\]
The cyclic language-rank recoding is
\[
\Fold_{\beta,m}(w)=
\bigl(\operatorname{Rank}_{\beta,m}|_{X_m^{(\beta)}}\bigr)^{-1}
\left(\operatorname{Rank}_{\beta,m}(w)\bmod Q_m(\beta)\right).
\]
Finally,
\[
(\Phi_{\beta,m}(z))_t
=\Fold_{\beta,m}(z_t,\ldots,z_{t+m-1}),\qquad
Y_{\beta,m}=\Phi_{\beta,m}(\mathcal A_\beta^{\mathbb Z}).
\]
The nontrivial overlap threshold is
\[
m_*(\beta)=\min\{m\ge2:\Phi_{\beta,m}\text{ is a conjugacy onto the
SFT }Y_{\beta,m}\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Parry rank is consecutive and canonical]
\label{prop:parry-rank-bijection}
The language counts satisfy
\begin{align}
Q_0&=1,\quad Q_1=a+1,\quad Q_m=aQ_{m-1}+bQ_{m-2}
&& (P^-_{a,b},\ m\ge2),\label{eq:qminus}\\
Q_0&=1,\quad Q_1=a,\quad Q_m=aQ_{m-1}-bQ_{m-2}
&& (P^+_{a,b},\ m\ge2).\label{eq:qplus}
\end{align}
For every quadratic Pisot $\beta$ and $m\ge1$,
\[
\operatorname{Rank}_{\beta,m}|_{X_m^{(\beta)}}:
X_m^{(\beta)}\longrightarrow\{0,\ldots,Q_m(\beta)-1\}
\]
is an order-preserving bijection when $X_m^{(\beta)}$ is read in the
colexicographic order.  Thus Definition~\ref{def:quadratic-parry-fold} is
determined by the greedy language and its Parry word; it is not a choice of
an auxiliary enumeration.  For $P^-_{a,1}$ it is exactly
Definition~\ref{def:metallic-window-data}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
In the negative chamber, Parry admissibility reduces in the low-to-high
orientation to
\[
x_k=a\Longrightarrow x_{k-1}<b.
\]
We use induction on $m$, with the invariant that the ranks of $X_m^{(\beta)}$
form the initial interval $[0,Q_m-1]$.  It is immediate for $m=0,1$.  For
$m\ge2$, a high digit $h\in\{0,\ldots,a-1\}$ leaves an arbitrary word of
$X_{m-1}^{(\beta)}$ and hence contributes
\[
[hQ_{m-1},(h+1)Q_{m-1}-1].
\]
For high digit $a$, the next digit is
$g\in\{0,\ldots,b-1\}$ and the remaining word is arbitrary in
$X_{m-2}^{(\beta)}$; its ranks are
\[
aQ_{m-1}+[gQ_{m-2},(g+1)Q_{m-2}-1].
\]
The intervals are consecutive in colexicographic order and their union is
$[0,aQ_{m-1}+bQ_{m-2}-1]$.  This proves simultaneously the negative
recurrence, the induction invariant, and order preservation.

For the positive chamber put
\[
d=a-1,\qquad c_0=a-b-1,
\]
and define the boundary-bounded sublanguage
\[
B_m:=\{x\in X_m^{(\beta)}:
(x_m,\ldots,x_1)\le_{\rm lex}c_0^m\},
\qquad R_m:=|B_m|.
\]
We prove simultaneously, for every $m\ge0$, the coupled induction invariant
\begin{equation}
\Rank_{\beta,m}(X_m^{(\beta)})=[0,Q_m-1],
\qquad
\Rank_{\beta,m}(B_m)=[0,R_m-1].
\label{eq:coupled-rank-invariant}
\end{equation}
Here $X_0^{(\beta)}=B_0=\{\varnothing\}$, so $Q_0=R_0=1$ and the assertion
holds at $m=0$.  At $m=1$, one has $Q_1=d+1=a$ and
$R_1=c_0+1=a-b$, and the ranks are the stated intervals.

Assume \eqref{eq:coupled-rank-invariant} through length $m-1$.  Parry
admissibility says that a high digit $h<d$ may be followed by any word in
$X_{m-1}^{(\beta)}$, whereas a high digit $d$ must be followed by a word in
$B_{m-1}$.  The classes $h=0,\ldots,d-1$ therefore give the consecutive
intervals
\[
[hQ_{m-1},(h+1)Q_{m-1}-1],
\]
and the high class $h=d$ gives
\[
[dQ_{m-1},dQ_{m-1}+R_{m-1}-1].
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}
Q_m=dQ_{m-1}+R_{m-1},
\qquad
\Rank_{\beta,m}(X_m^{(\beta)})=[0,Q_m-1].
\label{eq:positive-X-coupling}
\end{equation}

The same decomposition inside $B_m$ has high digits
$0,\ldots,c_0-1$ followed by arbitrary words of $X_{m-1}^{(\beta)}$, and
high digit $c_0$ followed by a word of $B_{m-1}$.  Hence
\begin{equation}
R_m=c_0Q_{m-1}+R_{m-1},
\qquad
\Rank_{\beta,m}(B_m)=[0,R_m-1].
\label{eq:positive-B-coupling}
\end{equation}
This closes the simultaneous induction and proves consecutiveness rather than
assuming it.  Subtracting \eqref{eq:positive-B-coupling} from
\eqref{eq:positive-X-coupling} gives
\[
Q_m-R_m=(d-c_0)Q_{m-1}=bQ_{m-1}.
\]
Thus, for $m\ge2$,
\[
R_{m-1}=Q_{m-1}-bQ_{m-2}
\]
and
\[
Q_m=dQ_{m-1}+R_{m-1}
=(d+1)Q_{m-1}-bQ_{m-2}
=aQ_{m-1}-bQ_{m-2},
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:qplus}.  The order of the displayed digit classes is
the colexicographic order, so the same induction proves order preservation.
When $b=1$ in the negative chamber, the rule and recurrence are precisely
those of Definition~\ref{def:metallic-window-data}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The bounded sliding-congruence lemma}

The separation estimate used in the sliding argument is isolated first.  In
particular, the integer multiple and the error term are both retained.

\begin{lemma}[Nearest-multiple separation]
\label{lem:nearest-multiple-separation}
Let $Q_0,Q_1,\ldots$ satisfy either \eqref{eq:qminus} or \eqref{eq:qplus},
write $s=1$ or $s=-1$ accordingly, and put
\[
d=\begin{cases}a,&s=1,\\a-1,&s=-1.\end{cases}
\]
Then, for $r\ge4$ and $1\le |e|\le d$,
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{dist}(beQ_{r-1},Q_r\mathbb Z)\ge Q_{r-2}.
\label{eq:quadratic-separation}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Distance is unchanged by replacing $e$ with $-e$, so assume $1\le e\le d$.
Set
\[
R_r:=\frac{Q_{r-1}}{Q_{r-2}}.
\]
The recurrence gives $R_{r+1}=a+sb/R_r$.  Its initial values and the parameter
ranges imply, by induction,
\begin{align}
a+\frac{b}{a+1}&\le R_r<a+\frac ba &&(s=1,\ r\ge3),
\label{eq:ratio-plus}\\
a-\frac{b}{a-1}&<R_r\le a-\frac ba &&(s=-1,\ r\ge3).
\label{eq:ratio-minus}
\end{align}
For completeness, in the positive-recurrence case the map
$x\mapsto a+b/x$ reverses order, sends
$[a+b/(a+1),a+b/a)$ into itself, and $R_3=a+b/(a+1)$.
In the negative-recurrence case $x\mapsto a-b/x$ preserves order, the interval
in \eqref{eq:ratio-minus} lies in $(a-1,a)$, and $R_3=a-b/a$.
These observations prove the two inductions, including the stated strict
endpoints.

We shall also use the following sharpened bounds, obtained by applying the
same recurrence once more:
\begin{align*}
L_+&:=a+\frac{b}{a+b/(a+b/(a+1))},&
U_+&:=a+\frac{b}{a+b/(a+1)},\\
L_-&:=a-\frac{b}{a-1},&
U_-&:=a-\frac{b}{a-b/a}.
\end{align*}
Thus
\begin{equation}
L_+\le R_r\le U_+\quad(s=1,r\ge4),
\qquad
L_-<R_r\le U_-\quad(s=-1,r\ge4).
\label{eq:sharpened-ratio-bounds}
\end{equation}
The first assertion follows because the order-reversing map interchanges the
endpoints $R_4=U_+$ and $R_5=L_+$ and maps $[L_+,U_+]$ into itself.  The
second follows because $R_3=a-b/a$, $R_4=U_-$, and the increasing map sends
$(L_-,U_-]$ into itself.

Choose a nearest integer $k$ to
\[
z:=\frac{beQ_{r-1}}{Q_r}=\frac{be}{R_{r+1}}.
\]
The lower bounds $R_{r+1}>a$ for $s=1$ and $R_{r+1}>a-1$ for $s=-1$ give
\[
0<z<b.
\]
Indeed $e\le a$ in the first case and $e\le a-1$ in the second.  Hence every
nearest integer satisfies
\begin{equation}
0\le k\le b.
\label{eq:nearest-k-bound}
\end{equation}
Put $h:=be-ak$.  The exact error, with no omitted remainder, is
\begin{align}
E&:=beQ_{r-1}-kQ_r\notag\\
 &=(be-ak)Q_{r-1}-skbQ_{r-2}
   =(hR_r-skb)Q_{r-2}.
\label{eq:nearest-error}
\end{align}

We first record the bounded integer exclusion for the cancelling sign in the
positive recurrence.  For $1\le e\le a$, $0\le k\le b$, and $h=be-ak$,
\begin{equation}
h>0\Longrightarrow
  hL_+-kb\ge1\quad\hbox{or}\quad kb-hU_+\ge1.
\label{eq:endpoint-plus}
\end{equation}
Write $j=kb-ah$.  Since $h=be-ak$, solving for $(e,k)$ gives
\[
k=\frac{ah+j}{b},\qquad
e=\frac{(a^2+b)h+aj}{b^2}.
\]
Thus the two displayed numerators are divisible by $b$ and $b^2$,
respectively.  We give the remaining Euclidean divisions explicitly.  Write
\[
be=aq+r,\qquad qb=ap+t,\qquad 0\le r,t<a.
\]
If $k\le q-1$, then $h\ge a+r$ and
\[
hL_+-kb>(a+r)a-(b-1)b\ge1.
\]
If $k\ge q+1$, then $h<0$, so this case is not in the hypothesis of
\eqref{eq:endpoint-plus}.  Hence only $k=q$ remains, and then $h=r$.
Now $j=a(p-r)+t$.  The cases $p<r$ and $p>r$ give, respectively,
$hL_+-kb\ge1$ and $kb-hU_+\ge1$.  Explicitly, when $p<r$,
\[
rL_+-qb=a(r-p)-t+r(L_+-a)>a-t\ge1,
\]
whereas, when $p>r$, the bounds $0<U_+-a<b/a$ and $r<a$ give
\[
qb-rU_+=a(p-r)+t-r(U_+-a)>a-\frac{rb}{a}\ge1.
\]
When $p=r$, put $w=rb-at$.  The two division identities give
\begin{equation}
b^2e=r(a^2+b)+at,\qquad w=r(a^2+2b)-b^2e.
\label{eq:plus-terminal-divisions}
\end{equation}
The integer $w$ is nonzero.  To verify this without a hidden coprimality
assumption, suppose $w=0$ and write $a=gA$, $b=gB$ with
$\gcd(A,B)=1$.  From $at=rb$ one obtains $r=AR$ and $t=BR$ with
$0<R<g$.  Reducing $be=aq+r$ and $qb=ar+t$ modulo $g$ gives
$g\mid AR$ and $g\mid BR$.  Bezout's identity gives $g\mid R$, a
contradiction.  Substitution of
\eqref{eq:plus-terminal-divisions}, followed by multiplication by the positive
denominators, gives the exhaustive terminal alternatives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
w>0& rb(a^2+a+b)\ge(t+1)(a^3+a^2+2ab+b),\\
w<0& t(a^2+a+b)\ge rb(a+1)+(a^2+a+b).
\end{array}
\]
There is no ratio estimate hidden in this table.  Indeed,
\[
U_+-a=\frac{b(a+1)}{a^2+a+b},\qquad
L_+-a=\frac{b(a^2+a+b)}{a^3+a^2+2ab+b}.
\]
Thus the first row is exactly $r(L_+-a)-t\ge1$, after multiplication by
its positive denominator, and the second is exactly
$t-r(U_+-a)\ge1$.  The signs are exhaustive because $w\ne0$; the two
identities in \eqref{eq:plus-terminal-divisions} retain every quotient and
remainder used in clearing the denominators.  This proves
\eqref{eq:endpoint-plus}.

The cancelling sign for the negative recurrence has a shorter proof which
avoids Euclidean endpoint bookkeeping.  Let $\beta$ and $\alpha$ be the
roots of $x^2-ax+b$, with $0<\alpha<1<\beta$, and put
$g=-h=ak-be>0$.  The closed formula for the recurrence gives
\[
R_r=\frac{\beta^r-\alpha^r}{\beta^{r-1}-\alpha^{r-1}}>\beta,
\]
while \eqref{eq:sharpened-ratio-bounds} gives $R_r\le U_-$.  Consider the
nonzero integral norm
\[
\nu:=k^2-aek+be^2=(k-e\alpha)(k-e\beta).
\]
Here $k\le b\le a-2<\beta\le e\beta$, so the second factor is negative.

If $\nu<0$, then $k-e\alpha>0$, and $b=\alpha\beta$ and
$\beta^2=a\beta-b$ give
\[
g\beta-kb=\beta^2(k-e\alpha)
=\frac{\beta^2|\nu|}{e\beta-k}>1;
\]
the last inequality uses $e\le a-1<\beta$.  Hence $gR_r-kb>1$.

Suppose $\nu>0$ and set $\delta=e\alpha-k>0$.  Then
\[
g=e\alpha^2-a\delta>0,
\qquad
\nu=\delta\{e(\beta-\alpha)+\delta\}\ge1.
\]
In particular
$0<\delta<e\alpha^2/a\le(a-1)\alpha^2/a<1$.  Put $D=a^2-b$ and
$H=(a-1)(\beta-\alpha)+1$.  Since $e\le a-1$, the norm identity gives
$\delta>H^{-1}$.  Moreover
\[
\alpha-\frac{ab}{D}=\frac{\alpha^3}{D},
\]
and therefore
\begin{align*}
kb-gU_-
&=\beta^2\delta-\frac{g\alpha^3}{D}\\
&=\delta\left(\beta^2+\frac{a\alpha^3}{D}\right)
  -\frac{e\alpha^5}{D}\\
&>\frac{\beta^2}{H}-\frac{(a-1)\alpha^5}{D}>1.
\end{align*}
For the final inequality, all margins are displayed:
\[
D-H=2\alpha^2+\alpha(\beta-1)+(\beta-1)>0
\]
and
\[
\beta^2-H=\beta-1-\alpha(1-\alpha)>(a-1)\alpha^5.
\]
Indeed $\alpha^5<\alpha$, while $b\le a-2$ is equivalent to
$\beta(1-\alpha)\ge2-\alpha>1$.  Thus
$(\beta^2-H)/H>(a-1)\alpha^5/D$.  Since $R_r\le U_-$, this case gives
$kb-gR_r>1$.

We now cover all signs explicitly.  If $s=1$ and $h<0$, then
\[
|hR_r-kb|=(-h)R_r+kb>1.
\]
If $h=0$, then $k\ge1$ (because $e\ge1$), and
$|hR_r-kb|=kb\ge1$.  If $h>0$, the two alternatives in
\eqref{eq:endpoint-plus}, together with
$L_+\le R_r\le U_+$, give $|hR_r-kb|\ge1$.

If $s=-1$ and $h>0$, then $hR_r+kb>1$.  If $h=0$, again $k\ge1$ and the
modulus is $kb\ge1$.  The case $h<0$ was proved directly above.
Thus in both chambers
\[
|hR_r-skb|\ge1.
\]
Equation~\eqref{eq:nearest-error} now yields $|E|\ge Q_{r-2}$, which is
\eqref{eq:quadratic-separation}.
\end{proof}

The following sliding lemma is the arithmetic core of the block decoder.

\begin{lemma}[Quadratic bounded sliding congruences]
\label{lem:quadratic-sliding-congruences}
Take either parameter chamber in
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-pisot-chambers}, let $d=\lfloor\beta\rfloor$, and
let $(Q_j)$ be \eqref{eq:qminus} or \eqref{eq:qplus}.  If $m\ge3$ and
$e_0,\ldots,e_{2m-2}\in[-d,d]\cap\mathbb Z$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}Q_j e_{t+j}\equiv0\pmod{Q_m}
\qquad(0\le t<m),\label{eq:sliding-kernel}
\end{equation}
then $e_0=\cdots=e_{2m-2}=0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $s=1$ in the negative chamber and $s=-1$ in the positive chamber, so
$Q_{j+2}=aQ_{j+1}+sbQ_j$, and put
$\delta=Q_1-a$; hence $(d,\delta)=(a,1)$ for $s=1$ and
$(d,\delta)=(a-1,0)$ for $s=-1$.  Subtracting $a$ times the congruence at
$t+1$ and $sb$ times that at $t+2$ from the congruence at $t$ cancels every
interior coefficient and gives
\begin{equation}
e_t+\delta e_{t+1}-sbQ_{m-1}e_{t+m+1}\equiv0\pmod{Q_m}.
\label{eq:quadratic-elimination}
\end{equation}

Suppose first that $m\ge4$.  The small part of
\eqref{eq:quadratic-elimination} has modulus at most
$d(1+\delta)$.  On the other hand,
\[
Q_{m-2}\ge Q_2=
\begin{cases}
a^2+a+b>2a=d(1+\delta),&s=1,\\
a^2-b>a-1=d(1+\delta),&s=-1.
\end{cases}
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:nearest-multiple-separation} therefore gives a strictly larger
distance whenever $e_{t+m+1}\ne0$.  Hence
$e_{t+m+1}=0$ for $0\le t\le m-3$.  Thus
$e_{m+1}=\cdots=e_{2m-2}=0$.  The final original congruence reduces to
\[
e_{m-1}+Q_1e_m\equiv0\pmod{Q_m}.
\]
Its left side has modulus at most $d(1+Q_1)<Q_m$ and $Q_1>d$, so both
digits vanish.  Back substitution in the preceding congruences then gives
$e_{m-2},\ldots,e_0=0$ successively.

It remains to check $m=3$, where endpoint equality in the separation bound
can occur.  Here each integer sum in \eqref{eq:sliding-kernel} has modulus
less than $2Q_3$, so it is $k_tQ_3$ with $k_t\in\{-1,0,1\}$.  Substituting
the three values of $t$ gives
\begin{equation}
e_t+Q_1e_{t+1}+Q_2e_{t+2}=k_tQ_3,
\qquad t=0,1,2.
\label{eq:quadratic-m3-equalities}
\end{equation}
We now eliminate the two conjugate signs separately.

Suppose first that $s=1$.  Thus $d=a$ and
\[
(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3)
=(a+1,a^2+a+b,a^3+a^2+2ab+b).
\]
Consider one equation $x+Q_1y+Q_2z=kQ_3$ occurring in
\eqref{eq:quadratic-m3-equalities}.  By symmetry it suffices to treat
$k=0,1$.  If $k=0$, then $|z|\ge2$ is impossible because
$2Q_2>a(1+Q_1)$.  The choice $z=0$ gives $x=y=0$, while $z=1$ gives
\[
x+b+(a+1)(y+a)=0.
\]
Since $y+a\ge0$ and $-(x+b)\le a-b<a+1$, this forces
$(x,y,z)=(-b,-a,1)$; the case $z=-1$ is its negative.  If $k=1$ and
$z\le a-1$, then
\[
x+Q_1y+Q_2z
\le a+aQ_1+(a-1)Q_2
=Q_3-\bigl(b(a+2)-a\bigr)<Q_3.
\]
Hence $z=a$, after which $x+(a+1)y=b(a+1)$ forces $(x,y)=(0,b)$.
Consequently every bounded solution of one equation is
\[
(x,y,z;k)\in
\{(0,0,0;0),\ \pm(b,a,-1;0),\ \pm(0,b,a;1)\}.
\]
The terminal pairs of these triples are
$(0,0)$, $\pm(a,-1)$, and $\pm(b,a)$.  If $e_4\ne0$ and the $t=2$
triple is $\pm(0,b,a)$, its initial pair $\pm(0,b)$ cannot be a terminal
pair of the $t=1$ triple.  If instead the $t=2$ triple is
$\pm(b,a,-1)$, the overlap forces the $t=1$ triple to be
$\pm(0,b,a)$, whose initial pair $\pm(0,b)$ cannot be a terminal pair of
the $t=0$ triple.  Both alternatives are impossible, and therefore
$e_4=0$.

Suppose next that $s=-1$.  Put $C=a-b$ and $d=a-1$; then
$2\le C\le d$ and
\[
(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3)=(a,a^2-b,a^3-2ab).
\]
For one equation $x+ay+Q_2z=kQ_3$, again it suffices to take $k=0,1$.
When $k=0$, the inequality $2Q_2>d(1+a)=a^2-1$ gives $|z|\le1$.
The choice $z=0$ gives $x=y=0$, whereas $z=1$ gives
\[
x-b+a(y+a)=0.
\]
Here $1\le y+a\le2a-1$ and $b-x\le b+a-1\le2a-3$, so necessarily
$y+a=1$ and $x=b-a=-C$; the case $z=-1$ is the negative solution.
For $k=1$, if $z\le a-2$, then
\[
x+ay+Q_2z
\le d(1+a)+(a-2)Q_2
=Q_3-\bigl(a(a-b)-2b+1\bigr)<Q_3,
\]
because $a-b\ge2$.  Thus $z=d$, and
\[
x+ay=a(a-b)-b=aC-b.
\]
Reduction modulo $a$, together with $|x|\le a-1$, leaves precisely
$(x,y)=(-b,C)$ and $(x,y)=(C,C-1)$.  Hence the complete list is
\[
(x,y,z;k)\in
\{(0,0,0;0),\ \pm(C,d,-1;0),\
  \ \pm(-b,C,d;1),\ \pm(C,C-1,d;1)\}.
\]
Its terminal pairs are $(0,0)$, $\pm(d,-1)$, $\pm(C,d)$, and
$\pm(C-1,d)$.  Since $2\le C\le d$, neither $\pm(-b,C)$ nor
$\pm(C,C-1)$ occurs in this list of terminal pairs.  Thus a $t=2$ triple
of either of the last two types cannot overlap a $t=1$ triple.  The only
remaining nonzero possibility is $\pm(C,d,-1)$; it forces the $t=1$
triple to be $\pm(-b,C,d)$, whose initial pair $\pm(-b,C)$ cannot overlap
a $t=0$ triple.  Therefore $e_4=0$ also in this chamber.

In either sign, every nonzero triple in the corresponding list has nonzero
last coordinate.  It follows successively from the equations at
$t=2,1,0$ that $e_2=e_3=e_4=0$, then $e_1=0$, and finally $e_0=0$.
Thus the kernel is trivial also at $m=3$.  The finite computation described in
the data-availability statement includes this case as regression testing; it
is not used as proof of the parameter-uniform statement.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Sharp threshold and extremal bases}

\begin{theorem}[Full quadratic-Pisot cyclic-rank threshold]
\label{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold}
Let $\beta$ be an arbitrary quadratic Pisot number and use exactly the
greedy language, Parry data, rank, cyclic modulus and fold of
Definition~\ref{def:quadratic-parry-fold}.  Then
\[
m_*(\beta)=
\begin{cases}
3,&\beta\text{ is the root of }x^2-ax-a,\quad a\ge1,\\
3,&\beta\text{ is the root of }x^2-ax+1,\quad a\ge3,\\
2,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
More strongly, for every $m\ge m_*(\beta)$ and every $n\ge m$, the
finite-block sliding fold is injective and
\begin{equation}
|\mathcal L_n(Y_{\beta,m})|
=(\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1)^{n+m-1}.
\label{eq:quadratic-pisot-block-count}
\end{equation}
At these apertures $\Phi_{\beta,m}$ is a topological conjugacy from the full
$(\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1)$-shift onto the SFT $Y_{\beta,m}$, with inverse of
memory zero and anticipation $m-1$.

Consequently the maximum of the threshold function on the full quadratic
Pisot family is three.  Its extremizers are exactly the negative-conjugate
diagonal $P^-_{a,a}$ and the positive-conjugate norm-one family
$P^+_{a,1}$.  The golden mean is the least extremizer, but it is not the
unique extremizer after passage from metallic units to all quadratic Pisot
bases.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Equality of two folded output blocks is, by
Proposition~\ref{prop:parry-rank-bijection}, equivalent to the sliding
congruences \eqref{eq:sliding-kernel} for their digit differences.  For
$m\ge3$, Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-sliding-congruences} makes every
length-$m$ finite-block map injective.  Consecutive decoded blocks cover a
longer raw block, proving injectivity for every $n\ge m$ and the count
\eqref{eq:quadratic-pisot-block-count}.  The standard gluing argument used in
Theorem~\ref{thm:metallic-threshold-classification} then gives a local inverse
and an SFT description by forbidden output words of length at most $m+1$.

It remains to classify $m=2$.  Put
\[
\kappa=Q_2-dQ_1=
\begin{cases}b,&P^-_{a,b},\\ a-b,&P^+_{a,b}.
\end{cases}
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:parry-rank-bijection} gives the same explicit rule in
both chambers:
\[
\Fold_{\beta,2}(u,v)=
\begin{cases}
(u,v),&v<d\text{ or }u<\kappa,\\
(u-\kappa,0),&v=d\text{ and }u\ge\kappa.
\end{cases}
\]
If $d=\kappa$, the two constant raw points
$0^{\mathbb Z}$ and $d^{\mathbb Z}$ both map to the constant zero output,
so conjugacy fails.  This occurs exactly for $P^-_{a,a}$ and $P^+_{a,1}$.

Now assume $d>\kappa$, which is equivalent to $a>b$ in the negative chamber
and to $b>1$ in the positive chamber.  We prove finite-block injectivity,
including the boundary digits, rather than inferring it from a two-sided
inverse.  Let a raw triple $(a_0,a_1,a_2)$ produce
\[
y_i=(p_i,q_i)=\Fold_{\beta,2}(a_i,a_{i+1}),\qquad i=0,1.
\]
First recover the central digit from the two output symbols:
\begin{equation}
a_1=
\begin{cases}
q_0,&q_0>0,\\
0,&q_0=0\text{ and }p_1=0,\\
d,&q_0=0\text{ and }p_1\in\{d-\kappa,d\}.
\end{cases}
\label{eq:m2-central-decoder}
\end{equation}
Indeed, $q_0=0$ implies $a_1\in\{0,d\}$.  If $a_1=0$, the next pair has
first output coordinate $p_1=0$.  If $a_1=d$, then $p_1=d$ when
$a_2<d$ and $p_1=d-\kappa$ when $a_2=d$.  The alternatives are disjoint
because $d>\kappa>0$.

Having found $a_1$, recover the left boundary digit by
\begin{equation}
a_0=
\begin{cases}
p_0,&q_0>0,\\
p_0,&q_0=0\text{ and }a_1=0,\\
p_0+\kappa,&q_0=0\text{ and }a_1=d.
\end{cases}
\label{eq:m2-left-decoder}
\end{equation}
The last line is exactly the wrapped case in the explicit fold rule.  Finally,
recover the right boundary digit by
\begin{equation}
a_2=
\begin{cases}
q_1,&q_1>0,\\
0,&q_1=0\text{ and }p_1=a_1,\\
d,&q_1=0\text{ and }p_1=a_1-\kappa.
\end{cases}
\label{eq:m2-right-decoder}
\end{equation}
When $q_1=0$, the raw digit $a_2$ is $0$ or $d$; these give the last two
lines, which are disjoint because $\kappa>0$.  Equations
\eqref{eq:m2-central-decoder}--\eqref{eq:m2-right-decoder} prove directly that
\[
\Phi_{\beta,2,2}:\mathcal A_\beta^3
\longrightarrow (X_2^{(\beta)})^2
\]
is injective.

For any $n\ge2$, every consecutive pair $(y_t,y_{t+1})$ decodes the raw
triple $(a_t,a_{t+1},a_{t+2})$.  These triples cover the entire raw block
$a_0\ldots a_{n+1}$, so $\Phi_{\beta,2,n}$ is injective and
$|\mathcal L_n(Y_{\beta,2})|=(d+1)^{n+1}$.  On trajectories, using the first
coordinate of the triple decoded from $(y_t,y_{t+1})$ gives a genuine
memory-zero, anticipation-one inverse.

For the two extremal loci, Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-sliding-congruences} shows
that aperture three succeeds.  The chamber classification is exhaustive by
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-pisot-chambers}, completing the proof.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Arithmetic identifiability and optimal local structure}

The threshold classification leaves three finer questions: whether a fixed
aperture identifies the parameter chamber, how many consecutive output
symbols are needed by a causal inverse, and whether the finite-block and
finite-type bounds in Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold} are
sharp.  We answer the first and third completely.  For the causal question we
obtain the exact positive-chamber value and the exact negative-chamber value
at aperture three; the parameter-uniform negative-chamber value at larger
apertures remains an explicit interface.

\begin{theorem}[Aperture-two chamber duality and first separation]
\label{thm:quadratic-aperture-two-duality}
Let $q\ge3$ and $2\le\kappa\le q-1$, and let
\begin{align*}
\beta^-_{q,\kappa}&>1,
& (\beta^-_{q,\kappa})^2-(q-1)\beta^-_{q,\kappa}-\kappa&=0,\\
\beta^+_{q,\kappa}&>1,
& (\beta^+_{q,\kappa})^2-q\beta^+_{q,\kappa}+(q-\kappa)&=0.
\end{align*}
After identifying both digit alphabets with $\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$, their
aperture-two legal languages, ranks, folds, and sliding recodings coincide
pointwise.  Explicitly,
\[
Q_0=1,\qquad Q_1=q,\qquad Q_2=q(q-1)+\kappa,
\]
and
\[
X_2=\{(u,v):v<q-1\ \hbox{or}\ u<\kappa\},
\qquad
\Fold_2(u,v)=
\begin{cases}
(u,v),&v<q-1\ \hbox{or}\ u<\kappa,\\
(u-\kappa,0),&v=q-1\ \hbox{and}\ u\ge\kappa.
\end{cases}
\]
Moreover, these are all cross-chamber coincidences at aperture two: the pair
$(q,\kappa)$ is recovered from the digit alphabet and the fold, and its
equivalence class contains the displayed negative- and positive-conjugate
bases when $\kappa\ge2$.  For $\kappa=1$ only the negative-conjugate member
is a quadratic Pisot base in the parameter ranges of
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-pisot-chambers}.

The ambiguity is first resolved at aperture three.  In low-to-high
orientation,
\[
X_3^{(\beta^-_{q,\kappa})}
 \setminus X_3^{(\beta^+_{q,\kappa})}
=\{(h,\kappa-1,q-1):\kappa\le h\le q-1\},
\]
the reverse difference is empty, and
\[
Q_3(\beta^-_{q,\kappa})-Q_3(\beta^+_{q,\kappa})=q-\kappa.
\]
Thus the complete aperture-two input--output map does not determine the sign
of the conjugate, whereas the aperture-three legal language does.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For the negative chamber take $(a,b)=(q-1,\kappa)$; for the positive chamber
take $(a,b)=(q,q-\kappa)$.  The stated parameter bounds are precisely those
which place both choices in Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-pisot-chambers}.  In both
cases $d=q-1$, while Proposition~\ref{prop:parry-rank-bijection} gives
\[
Q_2=(q-1)q+\kappa=q^2-(q-\kappa).
\]
The two length-two Parry conditions both say that a high digit $q-1$ must be
followed, in the low-to-high convention, by a digit smaller than $\kappa$.
The displayed fold now follows directly from cyclic reduction of
$u+qv$ modulo $Q_2$.  This proves pointwise equality of the two sliding maps.

Conversely, the alphabet gives $q$, and the least $u$ for which
$(u,q-1)$ is sent to $(0,0)$ gives $\kappa$.  The chamber parametrization in
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-pisot-chambers} then leaves exactly the two displayed
members when $\kappa\ge2$ and only the negative member when $\kappa=1$.

Finally, the two quasi-greedy boundary words are
\[
d_{\beta^-}^*(1)=((q-1)(\kappa-1))^\infty,
\qquad
d_{\beta^+}^*(1)=(q-1)(\kappa-1)^\infty.
\]
Their first two digits agree.  At length three, the negative boundary permits
a suffix $(q-1,\kappa-1,h)$ for every $h\le q-1$, whereas the positive
boundary requires $h\le\kappa-1$.  All other suffix tests agree.  Reversing
to the low-to-high convention gives exactly the stated set difference.
There are $q-\kappa$ such words.  Equivalently, the two recurrences give
\[
Q_3^-=(q-1)Q_2+\kappa q,\qquad
Q_3^+=qQ_2-(q-\kappa)q,
\]
whose difference is $q^2-Q_2=q-\kappa$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Open negative-chamber two-window interface]
\label{rem:negative-two-window-open-interface}
For $a\ge b\ge1$ and $m\ge4$, the natural candidate statement is that two
consecutive congruences
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}Q_je_j\equiv
\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}Q_je_{j+1}\equiv0\pmod{Q_m},
\qquad |e_j|\le a,
\]
force $e_0=0$ for the recurrence
$Q_{j+2}=aQ_{j+1}+bQ_j$.  Finite enumeration supports this assertion, but a
parameter-uniform proof requires an exhaustive bounded-carry invariant.  In
particular, sorting only by the two multiples of $Q_m$ and then appealing to
the signs of successive quotient coefficients does not prove that all carry
branches have been covered.  We therefore do not use or claim this candidate
statement below.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Causal inverse bounds and the positive-chamber optimum]
\label{thm:quadratic-optimal-causal-inverse}
For $m\ge3$ define
\[
\ell_{\rm cau}(\beta,m)
=\min\{\ell\ge1:\ a_t=\psi(y_t,\ldots,y_{t+\ell-1})
\text{ for every }y=\Phi_{\beta,m}(a)\}.
\]
Then
\[
\ell_{\rm cau}(\beta,m)=3\quad(\beta'>0),
\qquad
\ell_{\rm cau}(\beta,3)=2\quad(\beta'<0).
\]
For $\beta'<0$ and $m\ge4$, the proved bounds are
\[
2\le \ell_{\rm cau}(\beta,m)\le m.
\]

If, explicitly, $(P)\subset\mathbb Z[z]$ denotes the principal ideal
generated by $P$ and
\[
\mathfrak a(P,d)=\min\{\deg H:0\ne H\in(P),\ H(0)\ne0,
\ \max_j|[z^j]H|\le d\},
\]
then
\[
\mathfrak a(P^-_{a,b},a)=2,
\qquad
\mathfrak a(P^+_{a,b},a-1)=3.
\]
Thus $\ell_{\rm cau}=\mathfrak a$ in the positive chamber for every
$m\ge3$ and in the negative chamber at $m=3$; equality in the negative
chamber for $m\ge4$ is precisely the interface in
Remark~\ref{rem:negative-two-window-open-interface}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose first that $P=P^-_{a,b}$, so $d=a$.  The coefficient vector
$(b,a,-1)$ of $-P$ is the difference of two digit blocks and has nonzero
first coordinate.  Padding it by zeros gives two raw length-$m$ words with
the same single output, so one output never suffices.  Conversely, equality
of two consecutive outputs at $m=3$ gives two overlapping triples from the
complete negative-chamber list in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-sliding-congruences}.  A triple in that list with
nonzero first coordinate is necessarily $\pm(b,a,-1)$; the next triple would
then begin with $\pm(a,-1)$, which is not the initial pair of any triple in
the list.  Hence $e_0=0$, and two outputs determine the first digit at
$m=3$.  For $m\ge4$, the lower bound remains two, while
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-sliding-congruences} shows that $m$ consecutive
outputs determine the entire overlapping raw block and hence its first digit.

Now let $P=P^+_{a,b}$, so $d=a-1$.  The polynomial
\[
(1+z)P(z)=b+(b-a)z+(1-a)z^2+z^3
\]
has all coefficients in $[-d,d]$ and nonzero constant term.  Its positive
and negative parts, padded by zeros, give two raw blocks with different first
digits and the same two consecutive outputs.  Indeed, the first weighted sum
is zero when $m\ge4$ and is $-Q_3$ when $m=3$, while the shifted sum is zero.
Thus two outputs do not suffice.

Three outputs do suffice.  For $m=3$ this is
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-sliding-congruences}.  For $m\ge4$, apply the
elimination leading to \eqref{eq:quadratic-elimination} to the first three
equal-output congruences.  Since here $s=-1$ and $\delta=0$, it gives
\[
e_0+bQ_{m-1}e_{m+1}\equiv0\pmod{Q_m}.
\]
If $e_{m+1}\ne0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:nearest-multiple-separation} makes the
distance of the second term from $Q_m\mathbb Z$ at least
$Q_{m-2}>a-1\ge|e_0|$, a contradiction.  Hence $e_{m+1}=0$, and then
$|e_0|<Q_m$ forces $e_0=0$.

Finally, no nonzero polynomial of degree below two belongs to $(P_\beta)$.
For $P^-_{a,b}$ the polynomial $-P^-_{a,b}$ has coefficient norm $a$, so
$\mathfrak a(P^-_{a,b},a)=2$.  For $P^+_{a,b}$ every degree-two member of
the integral ideal is a nonzero integral multiple of $P^+_{a,b}$ and has
coefficient norm at least $a>d$, while $(1+z)P^+_{a,b}$ has coefficient norm
at most $a-1$.  Hence $\mathfrak a(P^+_{a,b},a-1)=3$, proving the last
assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Critical two-fixed-point normal form]
\label{thm:quadratic-critical-normal-form}
Let $\beta$ be an extremizer in
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold}, put
$q=\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1$ and $d=q-1$, and consider its critical map
$\Phi_{\beta,2}$.  Then
\[
\Fold_{\beta,2}(u,v)=
\begin{cases}
(u,v),&(u,v)\ne(d,d),\\
(0,0),&(u,v)=(d,d).
\end{cases}
\]
Its only nonsingleton two-sided fiber is
\[
\Phi_{\beta,2}^{-1}((00)^{\mathbb Z})
=\{0^{\mathbb Z},d^{\mathbb Z}\}.
\]
Consequently
\[
h_{\rm top}(Y_{\beta,2})=\log q,
\qquad
\#\operatorname{Fix}(\sigma^n|_{Y_{\beta,2}})=q^n-1,
\qquad
\zeta_{Y_{\beta,2}}(z)=\frac{1-z}{1-qz}.
\]
The critical image is strictly sofic.  Its right Fischer cover has vertices
$0,\ldots,d$ and one edge $u\to v$ for every ordered pair; the edge label is
$(u,v)$ except that $d\to d$ is labeled $(0,0)$.  The cover is bi-resolving,
and the factor is one-to-one away from the two fixed points above.  Hence, in
the standard terminology, the critical image is a near-Markov AFT shift and
its multiplicity graph is $K_{2,1}$: the two exceptional domain orbits lie
over the single exceptional image orbit.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
At either extremal locus the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold} has $\kappa=d$, which gives
the displayed rule.  Every nonzero output symbol records its raw edge
uniquely and hence propagates the raw digits uniquely in both directions.
If every output symbol is $(0,0)$, each raw edge is either $0\to0$ or
$d\to d$; overlap forces one of the two constant paths.  This proves the
fiber statement.

The map is finite-to-one from the full $q$-shift, so entropy is $\log q$.
A point fixed by $\sigma^n$ outside the exceptional image has a unique
preimage and that preimage is fixed by $\sigma^n$.  The $q^n$ fixed points
of the full shift therefore map to $q^n-1$ fixed image points, since exactly
the two constant preimages are identified.  The zeta identity follows from
\[
\exp\left(\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(q^n-1)z^n}{n}\right)
=\frac{1-z}{1-qz}.
\]

The displayed graph is right- and left-resolving and follower-separated.
Every vertex is reached by a one-symbol label different from $(0,0)$, which
is intrinsically synchronizing.  Lemma~\ref{lem:fischer-cover-criterion}
therefore identifies it as the right Fischer cover.

To see that the image is not an SFT, fix $N$ and choose $L>N$.  The word
\[
(d,0)(0,0)^L(d,0)
\]
is not admissible: the first anchor forces the intervening hidden state to be
$0$, while the second requires it to be $d$.  Every subword of length at
most $N+1$ meets at most one anchor and is admissible, using the constant
$0$ or constant $d$ hidden path as appropriate.  Thus no finite forbidden
list defines the image.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact finite-block onset, Fischer cover, and Markov order]
\label{thm:quadratic-exact-local-order}
Let $m\ge m_*(\beta)$ and define
\[
\delta(\beta,m)=\min\{n\ge1:\Phi_{\beta,m,n}\text{ is injective}\}.
\]
Then
\[
\delta(\beta,m)=m.
\]
The natural overlap graph with vertex set
$\mathcal A_\beta^{m-1}$ and edge labels $\Fold_{\beta,m}$ is the right
Fischer cover of $Y_{\beta,m}$ and has exactly
$(\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1)^{m-1}$ vertices.  In the output alphabet fixed in
Definition~\ref{def:quadratic-parry-fold}, the image is an $m$-step SFT but
not an $(m-1)$-step SFT.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The upper bound $\delta(\beta,m)\le m$ is
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold}.  For $m\ge3$ the reverse
inequality has a uniform certificate.  In the negative chamber, place the
difference vector $(b,a,-1)$ in raw positions $m-2,m-1,m$ and zeros
elsewhere.  In the positive chamber place
$(b,b-a,1-a,1)$ in positions $m-3,\ldots,m$.  Each vector is the difference
of two digit blocks.  The recurrence shows that all $m-1$ consecutive output
ranks agree modulo $Q_m$, while the raw blocks differ.  For an invertible
aperture $m=2$, the two pairs $(0,0)$ and $(\kappa,d)$ have the same single
output, so again $\delta\ge m$.

The overlap graph is essential and irreducible because its underlying graph
is the full de Bruijn graph.  It is right-resolving: two edges with the same
initial vertex and different appended digits have rank difference
$hQ_{m-1}$ with $1\le|h|\le d$, which is nonzero modulo $Q_m$.  It is
left-resolving because two edges with the same terminal vertex and different
initial digits have nonzero rank difference of modulus at most $d<Q_m$.
By $\delta=m$, every output word of length $m$ labels a unique path and is
intrinsically synchronizing.  Distinct vertices have distinct follower
languages: a common right-infinite label would be decoded by
Theorem~\ref{thm:quadratic-optimal-causal-inverse} when $m\ge3$, or by
\eqref{eq:m2-central-decoder}--\eqref{eq:m2-right-decoder} when $m=2$, and
would force the two raw vertices to coincide.  The Fischer-cover criterion
now proves the cover assertion and its state count.

The gluing proof in Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold} defines
$Y_{\beta,m}$ by forbidden output words of length at most $m+1$, so it is an
$m$-step SFT.  The difference certificates above give a length-$(m-1)$
output word which labels two paths ending at distinct Fischer states; for
$m=2$ the same role is played by the common label $(0,0)$.  Since the states
have distinct follower languages, this word is not intrinsically
synchronizing.  Every word of length $r$ in an $r$-step SFT is intrinsically
synchronizing.  Hence $Y_{\beta,m}$ is not an $(m-1)$-step SFT.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Worked cases in both chambers}

The following computations use the low-to-high convention $(u,v)$ and show
the Parry boundary, the legal rank interval, the cyclic reduction, and the
threshold classification in four genuinely nonmetallic cases.

\begin{example}[Negative conjugate, extremal]
Let $\beta$ be the positive root of $x^2-2x-2$.  Here
$(a,b,d)=(2,2,2)$,
\[
d_\beta^*(1)=(21)^\infty,\qquad (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(1,3,8),
\qquad \kappa=b=2=d.
\]
At length two, legality is $v=2\Rightarrow u<2$.  Thus the legal pairs are
\[
(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(0,1),(1,1),(2,1),(0,2),(1,2),
\]
and their ranks $u+3v$ are exactly $0,\ldots,7$.  The raw pair $(2,2)$ has
rank $8$, so cyclic reduction modulo $Q_2=8$ gives
$\Fold_{\beta,2}(2,2)=(0,0)$.  Consequently the constant raw points
$0^{\mathbb Z}$ and $2^{\mathbb Z}$ collide at aperture two.  Theorem
\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold} gives $m_*(\beta)=3$, as predicted by
the negative extremal condition $a=b$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Negative conjugate, nonextremal]
Let $\beta$ be the positive root of $x^2-3x-2$.  Then
$(a,b,d)=(3,2,3)$,
\[
d_\beta^*(1)=(31)^\infty,\qquad (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(1,4,14),
\qquad \kappa=b=2<d.
\]
The legal pairs obey $v=3\Rightarrow u<2$; explicitly,
\[
X_2^{(\beta)}=\{0,1,2,3\}\times\{0,1,2\}
\ \cup\ \{(0,3),(1,3)\},
\]
and their ranks $u+4v$ fill $0,\ldots,13$.  The only wrapped pairs are
\[
\Fold_{\beta,2}(2,3)=(0,0),\qquad
\Fold_{\beta,2}(3,3)=(1,0).
\]
For the raw triple $(3,3,0)$ the two outputs are
$y_0=(1,0)$ and $y_1=(3,0)$.  Formula
\eqref{eq:m2-central-decoder} reads $p_1=3\in\{d-\kappa,d\}=\{1,3\}$ and
recovers $a_1=3$; then \eqref{eq:m2-left-decoder} gives
$a_0=1+2=3$, and \eqref{eq:m2-right-decoder} gives $a_2=0$ because
$p_1=a_1$.  Hence the boundary triple is recovered from two outputs and
$m_*(\beta)=2$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Positive conjugate, extremal]
Let $\beta$ be the positive root of $x^2-3x+1$.  Here
$(a,b,d,c_0)=(3,1,2,1)$,
\[
d_\beta^*(1)=21^\infty,\qquad (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(1,3,8),
\qquad \kappa=a-b=2=d.
\]
The boundary condition at length two is $v=2\Rightarrow u\le1$.  Hence the
legal pairs are
\[
(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(0,1),(1,1),(2,1),(0,2),(1,2),
\]
with ranks $0,\ldots,7$, while $(2,2)$ has rank $8$ and is recoded to
$(0,0)$.  The constant raw points $0^{\mathbb Z}$ and
$2^{\mathbb Z}$ therefore collide at aperture two.  This is the positive
norm-one extremal family $b=1$, and $m_*(\beta)=3$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Positive conjugate, nonextremal]
Let $\beta$ be the positive root of $x^2-4x+2$.  Then
$(a,b,d,c_0)=(4,2,3,1)$,
\[
d_\beta^*(1)=31^\infty,\qquad (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(1,4,14),
\qquad \kappa=a-b=2<d.
\]
The length-two boundary again gives $v=3\Rightarrow u\le1$, so the legal
ranks on
\[
X_2^{(\beta)}=\{0,1,2,3\}\times\{0,1,2\}
\ \cup\ \{(0,3),(1,3)\}
\]
are $0,\ldots,13$, and the wrapped pairs are
$(2,3)\mapsto(0,0)$ and $(3,3)\mapsto(1,0)$.  For the raw triple $(3,3,0)$,
the output pair $((1,0),(3,0))$ is decoded exactly as in the preceding
nonextremal example: $a_1=3$, $a_0=1+\kappa=3$, and $a_2=0$.  Thus the
positive-chamber nonextremal case has $m_*(\beta)=2$.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[What is and is not claimed]
\label{rem:quadratic-open-interface}
The theorem concerns the cyclic language-rank recoding of
Definition~\ref{def:quadratic-parry-fold}.  Published finite-transducer
normalization results for Pisot bases
\cite{Frougny1992,FrougnySteiner2008,BertheFrougnyRigoSakarovitch2019}
establish recognizability for numerical representations on other redundant
digit sets and boundary conventions, but they do not identify those
normalizations with this cyclic rank map.
No threshold claim is made for signed digits, non-greedy expansions,
non-cyclic truncation, degree greater than two, or general Pisot substitution
codings.  These choices are genuine residual interfaces rather than
consequences of Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold}.
\end{remark}
