1400:7 Comments and open questions
1401-
1402:In Section 5.2 we showed that p can be arbitrarily large for degree 6 Salem
1403-numbers. It would be interesting to investigate whether or not the same is true
1404-for m. The largest value of m found so far is m = 26440386599 which is achieved
1405:by the Salem polynomial P (x) = (-5, -2, -11). It may be possible to exhibit
1406:a family of degree 6 Salem numbers with arbitrarily large m in much the same
1407-way as we have here for p. While it appears that we have m = 1 for the large
1408:majority of degree 6 Salem numbers (at least for small trace), it seems that
1409-values of m > 1 occur with some regularity.
1410-
1411:    Another question that we can ask is, what more can we say about the co-
1412-factors of these expansions? In Section 3, we demonstrated a constant bound
1413-on the dn-1 coefficient. Perhaps other constant bounds exist on the other coef-
1414-ficients. Even without constant bounds, it may be possible to find bounds that
1415-are stronger than the ones outlined in Section 3 which would lend themselves
1416-well to the computation of these co-factors. Moreover, it would seem that there
1417-is a much richer structure to these co-factors in the case when m = 1. For

tmp\2401.07771.txt-4-
tmp\2401.07771.txt:5:                                                    Abstract. We provide a proof for one version of Pisot conjecture. We make
tmp\2401.07771.txt-6-                                                    use of the weak mixing property of the subshift of finite type derived from the
tmp\2401.07771.txt-7-                                                    prefix-suffix automaton to conclude that the substitution dynamical system has
tmp\2401.07771.txt:8:                                                    pure discrete spectrum.
tmp\2401.07771.txt-9-
tmp\2401.07771.txt-10-                                                                                1. Introduction
tmp\2401.07771.txt-11-
tmp\2401.07771.txt-12-                                             Recurrence is one of the main concerns in Ergodic theory. In this paper, we
tmp\2401.07771.txt-13-                                          study the classification of uniformly recurrent sequences generated by substitu-
tmp\2401.07771.txt-14-                                          tions, based on their spectral type.
tmp\2401.07771.txt-15-
tmp\2401.07771.txt:16:                                             There are a group of problems called Pisot conjecture to which we recom-
tmp\2401.07771.txt:17:                                          mend [1] as a general reference. Among various versions of Pisot conjecture and
tmp\2401.07771.txt-18-                                          related problems, we specifically address the followings.
tmp\2401.07771.txt-19-
tmp\2401.07771.txt:20:                                          Pisot Substitution Conjecture. If  is an irreducible Pisot substitution, then the
tmp\2401.07771.txt:21:                                          substitution dynamical system has pure discrete spectrum (or pure point spec-
tmp\2401.07771.txt-22-                                          trum).
tmp\2401.07771.txt-23-
tmp\2401.07771.txt:24:                                          Strong Coincidence Conjecture. Every irreducible Pisot substitution  satisfies
tmp\2401.07771.txt:25:                                          the strong coincidence condition.
tmp\2401.07771.txt-26-
tmp\2401.07771.txt:27:                                             We only mention known results which are directly related to these conjectures:
tmp\2401.07771.txt:28:                                          Barge and Diamond [2] proves Strong Coincidence Conjecture for two symbol
tmp\2401.07771.txt-29-                                          cases (n = 2 in our notation) and, using it, Hollander and Solomyak [10] solves
tmp\2401.07771.txt:30:                                          Pisot Substitution Conjecture for n = 2.
tmp\2401.07771.txt-31-
tmp\2401.07771.txt:32:                                             Our goal is to prove the two conjectures for general n  2 by a geometric
tmp\2401.07771.txt-33-                                          and number-theoretical approach combined with Ergodic theory. This `classical'
tmp\2401.07771.txt-34-                                          approach initiated by Rauzy [19] consists of constructing a geometric represen-
tmp\2401.07771.txt-35-                                          tation of the substitution dynamical system (the Rauzy fractal R and the domain
tmp\2401.07771.txt-36-                                          exchange transformation on it), and showing that it is measure-theoretically con-
tmp\2401.07771.txt-37-                                          jugate to an ergodic rotation of a compact abelian group.
tmp\2401.07771.txt-38-

tmp\2401.07771.txt-93-K з K by means of Theorem 3. These two aspects are compared to conclude
tmp\2401.07771.txt-94-the proof of tiling (Theorem 5).

tmp\1810.03500.txt-8-                                                   Abstract. -- We give a sufficient geometric condition for a subshift to be mea-
tmp\1810.03500.txt-9-                                                   surably isomorphic to a domain exchange and to a translation on a torus. And for
tmp\1810.03500.txt-10-                                                   an irreducible unit Pisot substitution, we introduce a new topology on the discrete
tmp\1810.03500.txt-11-                                                   line and we give a simple necessary and sufficient condition for the symbolic system
tmp\1810.03500.txt:12:                                                   to have pure discrete spectrum. This condition gives rise to an algorithm based on

This note is concerned with those real numbers  with the property that all sufficiently small
rational numbers have a purely periodic -expansion, that is, such that

(1.1)                         () > 0.

With this definition, we get that () = 1, while () = 0. As one could expect, Con-
dition (1.1) turns out to be very restrictive. We deduce from works of Akiyama [5] and
Schmidt [23] (see details in Proposition 2.1) that such real numbers  have to be Pisot units.
This means that  is both a Pisot number and a unit of the integer ring of the number field
it generates. Recall that a Pisot number is a real algebraic integer which is greater than 1
and whose Galois conjugates (different from itself) are all inside the open unit disc.

   One relevant property for our study is

             (F) : every x  Z[1/]  [0, 1) has a finite -expansion.

This property was introduced by Frougny and Solomyak in [14]. It then has been studied for
various reasons during the twenty last years. In particular, Akiyama [2] proved the following
unexpected result.

Theorem A. -- If  is a Pisot unit satisfying (F), then () > 0.
RATIONAL NUMBERS WITH PURELY PERIODIC -EXPANSION  3

   The fact that (F) plays a crucial role in the study of () looks somewhat puzzling but it
will become more transparent in the sequel.

   The results of Hama, Imahashi and Schmidt previously mentioned about - and -
expansions are actually more general and lead, using Proposition 2.1, to a complete
understanding of () when  is a quadratic number.

Theorem HIS. -- Let  > 1 be a quadratic number. Then, () > 0 if and only if  is a
Pisot unit satisfying (F). In that case, () = 1.

   Furthermore, quadratic Pisot units satisfying (F) have been characterized in a simple way:
they correspond to positive roots of polynomials x2 - nx - 1, n running along the posi-
tive integers. These exactly correspond to quadratic Pisot units whose Galois conjugate is
negative.

   First, we establish the converse of Theorem A for algebraic numbers of degree 3. This
provides a result similar to Theorem HIS in that case.

Theorem 1.1. -- Let  > 1 be a cubic number. Then, () > 0 if and only if  is a Pisot
unit satisfying (F).

   We recall that Pisot units of degree 3 satisfying (F) have been nicely characterized in [4]:
they correspond to the largest real roots of polynomials x3 - ax2 - bx - 1, with a, b integers,
a  1 and -1  b  a + 1.

   It is tempting to ask whether, in Theorem 1.1, Property (F) would imply that () = 1 as
it is the case for quadratic Pisot units. However, Akiyama [2] proved that such a result does
not hold. Indeed, he obtained that the smallest Pisot number , which is the real root of the
polynomial x3 - x - 1, satisfies 0 < () < 1. More precisely, it was proved in [8] that ()
is abnormally close to the rational number 2/3 since one has

                                          () = 0.666 666 666 086 · · · .

This intriguing phenomenon naturally leads to ask about the arithmetic nature of ().

   In this direction, we will prove that () is irrational as a particular instance of the following
result.

Theorem 1.2. -- Let  be a cubic Pisot unit satisfying (F) and such that the number field
Q() is not totally real. Then, () is irrational. In particular, 0 < () < 1.

   Note that in Theorem 1.2 the condition that  does not generate a totally real number
field is equivalent to the fact that the Galois conjugates of  are complex (that is, they belong
to C \ R). In all this note, a complex Galois conjugate of an algebraic number  denotes a
Galois conjugate that belongs to C \ R.

   The proofs of our results rely on some topological properties of the tiles of the so-called
Thurston tilings associated with Pisot units. We introduce the notion of spiral points for
compact subsets of C that turns out to be crucial for our study. The fact that () vanishes
for a cubic Pisot unit that does not satisfy (F) is a consequence of the fact that the origin
is a spiral point with respect to the central tile of the underlying tiling. Theorem 1.2 comes
from the fact that () cannot be a spiral point with respect to this tile, which provides a
quite unusual proof of irrationality.

                                                                 SUBSTITUTION CONJECTURE

                                                   Abstract. -- We give a sufficient geometric condition for a subshift to be mea-
                                                   surably isomorphic to a domain exchange and to a translation on a torus. And for

                                                   using different methods. And we also provide an example of S-adic system with pure
                                                   discrete spectrum everywhere.

                                            1. Introduction

   Sturmian systems are well-known examples of subshifts that are conjugate to trans-
lations on the torus R/Z. In 1982, Gérard Rauzy (see [Rauzy 1982]) gave a gener-
alization to higher dimension for the subshift generated by the infinite fixed point of
the Tribonnacci substitution:

                                              a  ab
                                             

                                                 b  ac .
                                             c  a

He constructed a compact subset of R2, that we call now Rauzy fractal, and that
has the property that it tiles the plane by translation. And we can define a domain
exchange on this Rauzy fractal which is measurably conjugate to the subshift, and
measurably conjugate to a translation on the two dimensional torus R2/Z2.

   In 2001, P. Arnoux and S. Ito (see [Arnoux Ito 2001]) generalized the work of
Rauzy to any irreducible unit Pisot substitution. They introduced a combinatorial
condition which is easy to check, called the strong coincidence, that permits to get a
measurable conjugacy between the subshift and a domain exchange, which is also a
finite extension of a translation on a torus.

   To obtain a measurable conjugacy between the subshift of an irreducible unit
Pisot substitution and a translation on a torus, several equivalent conditions
(super coincidence, Geometric coincidence) has been studied ([Ito Rao 2003,
Barge Kwapisz 2006]). This article gives another formulation of such coincidences
YET ANOTHER CHARACTERIZATION OF THE PISOT SUBSTITUTION CONJECTURE  3

and a short proof of its equivalence. The new criterion is checked by automata

computation.
   We introduce a topology on Zd that permits to characterize easily when the subshift

of a given irreducible unit Pisot substitution over d letters is measurably isomorphic to

a translation on a (d - 1)-dimensional torus: see theorem 3.3. And we show that this

condition is equivalent to the non-emptiness of some computable regular language:

see theorem 5.12.

In the last section, we use this condition to prove the pure discreteness for the

family of substitution

                              a  akbc
                             
                        sk : b  c
                              ca

for k  N, where ak means that the letter a is repeated k times. And we also prove
the pure discreteness of the family of substitution

                               a  albak-l
                              
                        sl,k : b  c
                               ca

for k  N1, 0  l  k, by computing explicitly a automaton describing algebraic
relations, and showing that the pure discreteness for the substitution

                              a  akb
                             
                        sk : b  c
                              ca

implies the pure discreteness for the other substitutions.
   We also use the criterion to prove, for all word in SN , the pure discreteness of the

S-adic system with S = {,  }, where  and  are the two substitutions

arXiv:1912.10386v1 [math.NT] 22 Dec 2019  On the co-factors of degree 6 Salem number beta
                                                                 expansions

                                                                         Jacob J. Stockton
                                                               Department of Pure Mathematics

                                                                      University of Waterloo
                                                               Waterloo, ON, Canada, N2L 3G1
                                                                jacob.stockton@hotmail.com

                                                                        December 24, 2019

                                          Abstract

                                          For  > 1, a sequence (cn)n1  ZN+ with 0  cn <  is the beta
                                                                                    
                                          expansion of x with respect to  if x =    n=1  cn  -n .  Defining d(x) to

                                          be the greedy beta expansion of x with respect to , it is known that d(1)

                                          is eventually periodic as long as  is a Pisot number. It is conjectured

                                          that the same is true for Salem numbers, but is only currently known to

                                          be true for Salem numbers of degree 4. Heuristic arguments suggest that

                                          almost all degree 6 Salem numbers admit periodic expansions but that

                                          a positive proportion of degree 8 Salem numbers do not. In this paper,

                                          we investigate the degree 6 case. We present computational methods for

                                          searching for families of degree 6 numbers with eventually periodic greedy

                                          expansions by studying the co-factors of their expansions. We also prove

                                          that the greedy expansions of degree 6 Salem numbers can have arbitrarily

                                          large periods. In addition, computational evidence is compiled on the set

                                          of degree 6 Salem numbers with trace()  15. We give examples of

                                          numbers with trace()  15 whose expansions have period and preperiod
                                          lengths exceeding 1010, yet are still eventually periodic.

                                          MSC : Primary 11A63, Secondary 11R06
                                          Keywords: Salem numbers, beta expansions

                                          1 Introduction

                                          Beta expansions were first introduced by R´enyi [8] in 1957 as a generalization of
                                          the base-b representations of real numbers to non-integer bases. Suppose that

                                              Research partially supported by NSERC grant 2019-03930 and the University of Waterloo
                                          President's Research Award.

                                          1
 > 1 is a real number and (cn)n1 is an integer sequence with 0  cn <  such
that

                                                                      

                                          x = cn-n,

                                                                    n=1

for some x. Then the sequence (cn)n1 is said to be the beta expansion of x
with respect to . Note that beta expansions for a fixed x are not necessarily
unique; in fact, if  = (1 + 5)/2, then x = 1 has a (countably) infinite number
of distinct beta expansions. We therefore define the canonical "greedy" beta
expansion of x to be the largest beta expansion of x, ordered lexicographically.
The greedy expansion of a number x may be calculated by using a well-known
algorithm due to R´enyi: begin with r0 := x, and for n  1, set cn := rn-1
and rn := rn-1 - rn-1. Then (cn)n1 is the greedy beta expansion of x,
and we write d(x) := (cn)n1. In this paper, all beta expansions are assumed
to be greedy.

    One of the first questions that was asked about beta expansions was whether
or not the sequence of digits d(x) in the greedy expansion is eventually periodic.
More precisely, if there exists p  1 such that cn = cn+p for all n  1, then
the sequence (cn)n1 is said to be periodic. If (cn+m)n1 is periodic for some
m  0, then (cn)n1 is eventually periodic. For  > 1, R´enyi [8] and Parry
[7] studied the eventual periodicity of d(1) by considering the so-called beta
transformation T : [0, 1]  [0, 1) defined by

                                       T(x) := x mod 1.

Numbers for which the orbit {Tn(1)}n1 is finite are called Parry numbers (they
were called beta numbers by Parry). In the special case where TN (1) = 0 for
some N ,  is called a simple Parry number. Observe that in the algorithm
for calculating greedy beta expansions, one has rn = Tn(1) and hence  is
a Parry number if and only if d(1) is eventually periodic. In this case, the
smallest m  0 and p  1 such that cn+m = cn+m+p for all n  1 are called the
preperiod length and period length of the beta expansion, respectively. Note that
for simple Parry numbers, we have cn = 0 for all n  m and so (by ignoring
trailing zeros) these expansions can be considered to be finite. We therefore
define p = 0 for simple Parry numbers and write d(1) = c1, . . . , cm. When
p > 0, we instead write d(1) = c1, . . . , cm : cm+1, . . . , cm+p.

    Recall that a Pisot number (or sometimes Pisot-Vijayaraghavan number )
is an algebraic integer  > 1 whose Galois conjugates  all satisfy || < 1.
A Salem number is an algebraic integer  > 1 whose Galois conjugates  all
satisfy ||  1 with at least one conjugate satisfying || = 1. If  is Pisot or
Salem then its minimal polynomial P (x) may simply be referred to as a Pisot
or Salem polynomial, respectively.

    It was shown by Schmidt [10] that if all x  Q  [0, 1] have periodic -
expansions, then  is either a Pisot or a Salem number. Schmidt proved a
partial converse, which was independently proven by Bertrand [1], showing that
if  is Pisot then  is a Parry number. Schmidt conjectured that the same

                                                   2
was true for Salem numbers. In [2], Boyd answers this conjecture positively for
Salem numbers of degree 4; however, it is still not known for any degree greater
than 4. The degree 6 case already does not appear to be as well behaved as the
degree 4 case. In particular, one always has m + p < trace() for degree 4 Salem
numbers, but no similar bound seems to hold for degree 6 Salem numbers. Boyd
showed that the Salem number with minimal polynomial

P (x) = x6 - 3x5 - x4 - 7x3 - x2 - 3x + 1  (1.1)

has m + p > 1.1 × 109, presenting it as a possible counter-example to Schmidt's
conjecture. As part of this paper, we further this bound to m + p > 7.7 × 1010.

    It is straightforward to see that if  is a simple Parry number, i.e. with finite

expansion c1, . . . , cm, then  is an algebraic integer satisfying Pm() = 0, where
Pm(x) is defined by

Pm(x) := xm - c1xm-1 - · · · - cm.         (1.2)
these markers, a period can usually be detected by inspection unless the period

is unusually small. Of course, the use of the trailing coefficient of Bn here is
arbitrary, and any other suitable marker can be used.

7 Comments and open questions

In Section 5.2 we showed that p can be arbitrarily large for degree 6 Salem
numbers. It would be interesting to investigate whether or not the same is true
for m. The largest value of m found so far is m = 26440386599 which is achieved
by the Salem polynomial P (x) = (-5, -2, -11). It may be possible to exhibit
a family of degree 6 Salem numbers with arbitrarily large m in much the same
way as we have here for p. While it appears that we have m = 1 for the large
majority of degree 6 Salem numbers (at least for small trace), it seems that
values of m > 1 occur with some regularity.

    Another question that we can ask is, what more can we say about the co-
factors of these expansions? In Section 3, we demonstrated a constant bound
on the dn-1 coefficient. Perhaps other constant bounds exist on the other coef-
ficients. Even without constant bounds, it may be possible to find bounds that
are stronger than the ones outlined in Section 3 which would lend themselves
well to the computation of these co-factors. Moreover, it would seem that there
is a much richer structure to these co-factors in the case when m = 1. For
example, in Section 2.2 we showed that co-factors for such expansions have no
positive roots. Additionally, all co-factors with m = 1 which we have investi-
gated have been reciprocal, so it may be worthwhile to investigate whether or
not this is always the case.

stimulating discussions, and for his helpful feedback on the manuscript.

                                            "text":  "Nonlinear congruential pseudorandom numbers were introduced by \\textit{J. Eichenauer}, \\textit{H. Grothe} and \\textit{J. Lehn} [Metrika 35, 241-250 (1988))] in the following way. Let p be large prime and generate a sequence \\(y_ 0,y_ 1,..\\). of integers in \\(F_ p=\\{0,1,...,p-1\\}\\) by the recursion \\(y_{n+1}\\equiv f(y_ n)mod p\\) for \\(n=0,1,...\\), where f is an integer-valued function on \\(F_ p\\) such that the sequence of \\(y_ n\\) is purely periodic with period \\(p\\) and \\(\\{y_ 0,y_ 1,...,y_{p- 1}\\}=F_ p\\). Then the pseudorandom numbers \\(x_ n\\) are obtained by \\(x_ n=y_ n/p\\). The following equivalent description was given by the author [Metrika (to appear)]: there exists a uniquely determined polynomial \\(g\\) over the finite field \\(F_ p\\) such that \\(y_ n=g(n)\\) for all \\(n\\in F_ p\\) and \\(1\\leq s:=\\deg (g)\\leq p-2\\), where \\(\\{g(0),g(1),...,g(p-1)\\}=F_ p.\\) \n\n\nIn the present paper the behavior of these pseudorandom numbers under the \\(k\\)-dimensional serial test is investigated by considering the discrepancy \\(D_ N^{(k)}\\) of the points \\(\\bar x_ n=(x_ n,x_{n+1},...,x_{n+k-1})\\), \\(n=0,1,...,N-1\\). It is shown that \\(D_ p^{(k)}=O(sp^{-1/2}(\\log p)^ k)\\) for all \\(k\\leq s\\) and \\(D_ N^{(K)}=O(N^{-1}sp^{1/2}(\\log p)^{k+1})\\) for \\(1\\leq N\u003cp\\) and all \\(k\\leq s-1\\). It is also proved that these bounds are essentially best possible. As a consequence, nonlinear congruential pseudorandom numbers with an appropriate value of \\(s\\) have satisfactory statistical independence properties up to rather high dimensions.",

                                            "text":  "The present article deals with generalized \\(\\beta\\)-expansions. In particular, the authors construct natural extensions and show multiple tilings associated with them.\n\nLet \\(T: X\\to X\\) be defined by \\(Tx=\\beta x-a\\) for \\(x\\in X_a\\) and \\(a\\in A\\), where \\(A\\) is a finite subset of \\(\\mathbb{R}\\). This generalizes several kinds of transformations like the classical greedy \\(\\beta\\)-transformation, linear modulo \\(1\\) transformations, minimal weight expansions and symmetric \\(\\beta\\)-transformations.\n\nIn the first part they provide several properties of these transformation like admissibility, ordering, continuity. They also characterize when the shift space is sofic.\n\nThe second part deals with natural extensions. They start by characterizing those points which are eventually and purely periodic. Then they construct the natural extension and consider its domain. Finally they provide natural extensions for the different examples originating from the first part.\n\nIn the third part they consider multiple tilings. The authors provide a sufficient criterion for the presence of a multiple tiling of a hyperplane and of the torus. At the end of this part they construct such a multiple tiling.",

                                            "text":  "The dynamics of a piecewise isometry \\(T\\) with rotations by \\(2\\pi i/5\\) on a certain lozenge is studied. Using the fact that it has a self-inducing structure, it was shown in [\\textit{S. Akiyama} et al., Tsukuba J. Math. 32, No. 1, 197--251 (2008; Zbl 1209.37018)] that almost all points, in particular all points in \\(\\mathbb{Z}[\\zeta]\\), lie in pentagons with periodic orbits. The authors are interested in the dynamics of the aperiodic points. They are contained in the attractor of an iterated function system and are recognized by a Büchi automaton. The restriction of \\(T\\) to this attractor preserves the self-similar measure given by the IFS and is isomorphic to the 2-adic odometer. The orbit of each aperiodic point is uniformly distributed with respect to this measure. Moreover, the corresponding symbolic dynamical system is an \\(S\\)-adic shift given by a set of 4 substitutions. Points with purely periodic multiplicative coding are characterized with the help of a natural extension. Generalizations to other self-similar systems, in particular to a rotation by \\(4\\pi/7\\), and the role of Pisot numbers as scaling constants are discussed.",

                                                             "sign":  "Takao Komatsu (Hirosaki)"
                                                         },
                                            "text":  "This paper under review studies tilings and representation spaces related to the \\(\\beta\\)-transformation when \\(\\beta\\) is a Pisot number, that is not a unit. The obtained results are applied to study the set of rational numbers having a purely periodic \\(\\beta\\)-expansion. The authors make use of the connection between pure periodicity and a compact self-similar representation of number having no fractional part in their \\(\\beta\\)-expansion, called center tile. For elements \\(x\\) of the ring \\(\\mathbb Z[1/\\beta]\\), so-called \\(x\\)-tiles are introduced, so that the central tile is a finite union of \\(x\\)-tiles up to translation. These \\(x\\)-tiles provide a covering (and even in some cases a tiling) of the space the authors working in. This space, called complete representation space, is based on archimedean as well as on the non-archimedean completions of the number field \\(\\mathbb Q(b)\\) corresponding to the prime divisors of the norm of \\(\\beta\\). This representation space has numerous potential implications. The authors focus on the gamma function \\(\\gamma(\\beta)\\) defined as the supremum of the set of elements \\(v\\) in \\([0,1]\\) such that every positive rational number \\(p/q\\), with \\(p/q\\leq v\\) and \\(q\\) coprime with the norm of \\(\\beta\\), has a purely periodic \\(\\beta\\)-expansion. The key point relies on the description of the boundary of the tiles in terms of paths on a graph called ``boundary graph\u0027\u0027. The paper ends with explicit quadratic examples, showing that the general behaviour of \\(\\gamma(\\beta)\\) is slightly more complicated than in the unit case.",

                                                             "sign":  "Emil Grosswald (Philadelphia)"

                                            "text":  "Es handelt sich um eine im Nachlaß von I. Schur vorgefundene Arbeit, erstmals veröffentlicht in den Gesammelten Abhandlungen, die in ihrer Gesamtheit in diesem Zbl 0274.01054 besprochen wurden. \n\nThe paper discusses a complex of ideas centered around the concepts of periodic series and recurrent sequences; it consists of six chapters. \n\nChapter 1. A number sequence \\(\\{A_\\nu\\}\\) is said to be periodic, of period \\(h(=h(m))\\) modulo \\(m\\) if \n\\(A_{\\nu+h}\\equiv A_\\nu\\pmod m\\). For \\(m=p_1^{\\alpha_1}p_2^{\\alpha_2}\\cdots p_r^{\\alpha_r}\\), \\(h(m)=[h(p_1^{\\alpha_1}, \\ldots, h(p_r^{\\alpha_r})]\\) \\(([\\cdots] = \\) least common multiple). Let \\(\\mathfrak G(x) = A_0 + A_1x + \\ldots\\); then the sequence \\(\\{A_\\nu\\}\\) has period \\(h\\) modulo \\(p^\\alpha\\), if and only if \n\n\\[ \\mathfrak G(x) \\equiv (A_0 + \\ldots +A_{h-1}x^{h-1})/(1 -x^h) \\pmod{p^\\alpha}. \\] \n\nUsing a somewhat peculiar definition, it is proved that the periodicity of \\(x^n\\mathfrak G(x)\\) implies that of \\(x^m\\mathfrak G(x)\\) for \\(0\\le m\\le n\\) and that the periodicity of \\(\\mathfrak G(x)\\) and of \\(\\mathfrak H(x) = B_0 + B_1x + \\ldots\\)implies that of \\(\\mathfrak G(x) + \\mathfrak H(x)\\) and of \\(x\\mathfrak G(x)\\mathfrak H(x)\\), with the same period; furthermore, \\(A_0B_0 + A_1B_1x + \\ldots\\) also is periodic, with the same period. \n\nChapter 2 discusses recurrent sequences. Let \\(f(x) = x^n + \\sum_{\\mu=1}^n (-1)^\\mu c_\\mu x^{n-\\mu}\\), \\(c_\\mu\\in\\mathbb Z\\). A sequence \\(\\{A_\\nu\\}\\subset \\mathbb Z\\) is said to be recurrent, belonging to \\(f\\), or \\(f\\)-recurrent, if for \\(\\nu\\ge n\\), \\(\\sum_{\\mu=0}^n(-1)^\\mu c_\\mu A_{\\nu-\\mu} = 0\\). This happens if and only if \n\n\\[ \\left(\\sum_{\\mu=0}^n(-1)^\\mu c_\\mu t^\\mu\\right) \\mathfrak G(t) = \\sum_{\\lambda = 0}^{n-1} B_\\lambda t^\\lambda, \\] \n\nwith \\(\\mathfrak G(t) = A_+A_1t+\\ldots\\), \\(B_0 = A_0\\), \\(B_1 = A_1 - c_1A_0\\), \\(\\ldots\\), \\(B_{n-1} = A_{n-1} - c_1A_{n-2}+\\ldots\\pm c_{n-1}A_0\\). \n\nIf \\(\\psi(t) = \\left\\{\\sum_{\\mu=0}^n (-1)^\\mu c_\\mu t^\\mu\\right\\}^{-1} = \\sum_{m=0}^\\infty P_mt^m\\), then the \\(P_m\\) (``Wronskian functions\u0027\u0027) are \\(f\\)-recurrent and are polynomials in the \\(c_\\mu\\)\u0027s and also conversely. \n\nTheorem. The \\(n\\) sequences of coefficients \\(P_{\\nu - \\alpha}\\) \\((\\nu\\in\\mathbb Z, 0\\le \\alpha\\le n - 1)\\) corresponding to \\(t^\\alpha \\psi\\) form a fundamental system for the \\(f\\)-recurrent sequences. This means that one obtains all \\(f\\)-recurrent sequences, by setting \\(A_\\nu = B_0P_\\nu +B_1P_{\\nu-1}+ \\ldots + B_{n-1}P_{\\nu-n+1}\\) with arbitrary \\(B_j\\in\\mathbb Z\\). \n\nParticular case of \\(f\\)-recurrent sequences: the sums \\(s_\\nu = \\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^\\nu\\) of powers of the zeros of \\(f(x)\\). The main result of Chapter 3 is the \n\nTheorem: If \\(f(x) = x^n + a_1x^{n-1}+ \\ldots + a_n\\), \\((a_n,p) =1\\), then every \\(f\\)-recurrent sequence \\(\\{A_\\nu\\} \\bmod p^\\alpha\\) is purely periodical. If \\(p^\\rho \\le n - 1 \u003c p^{\\rho+1}\\), then the period \\(h \\bmod p^\\alpha\\) is a divisor of \\(p^{2\\alpha-2+\\alpha+\\rho}(p^M - 1)\\) (here \\(M=[1,2,\\ldots,n] = \\text{lcm}\\) of all integers \\(n)\\). In particular, the sequence \\(\\{s_\\nu\\}\\) has as period \\(h\\pmod{p^\\alpha}\\) a divisor of \\(p^{2\\alpha-2}(p^M-1)\\). If \\(a_n =\\pm 1\\), then every \\(f\\)-recurrent sequence is purely periodical. \n\nChapter 4 discusses periodic sequences that are not purely periodical, i.e., such that the periodicity \\(A_\\nu\\equiv A_{nu+h}\\pmod m\\) holds only for \\(\\nu\\ge  k(\u003e 0)\\). If \\(\\{A_\\nu\\} \\subset\\mathbb Z\\) is \\(f\\)-recurrent, \\(f = x^n + \\sum_{\\mu=1}^n a_\\mu x^{n-\\mu}\\) with \\(p\\mid a_n\\), then \\(\\{A_\\nu\\}\\) is not purely periodic \\(\\bmod {p^\\alpha}\\) \\((1\\le \\alpha\\in\\mathbb Z)\\). \n\nChapter 5 contains additional remarks concerning \\(f\\)-recurrent sequences. Its main result is the \n\nTheorem: Let \\(D\\) be the discriminant of \\(f(x)\\), let \\(p\\nmid D\\) and \\(f(x) \\equiv F_1F_2\\cdots F_r \\pmod p\\); then the period of every \\(\\bmod p^\\alpha\\) \\(f\\)-recurrent sequence is equal to that of the corresponding \\(F_1F_2\\cdots F_r)\\)-recurrent sequence. \n\nChapter 6 discusses general properties of periodic sequences. Clearly (1) \\(k\\mid \\ell \\Rightarrow h(k)\\mid h(\\ell)\\), and (2) \\([k, \\ell] = m \\Rightarrow [h(m)=[h(k),h(\\ell)]\\); in particular, \\(h(p^\\alpha)\\mid h(p^{\\alpha+\\lambda})\\) for \\(\\lambda \u003e0\\). If, from some point on, \\(h(p^\\alpha\\) remains constant, then the sequence \\(\\{A_\\nu\\}\\) is ``absolutely periodic\u0027\u0027, i.e., it consists of the subsequence \\(A_0,A_1,\\ldots,A_{n-1}\\) repeated indefinitely, \\(A_r =  A_s\\) for \\(r\\equiv s\\pmod h\\) and, for every \\(m\\), \\(h(m)\\mid h\\). \n\nTheorem: If \\(h(m)\\) is an arithmetical function that satisfies (1) and (2), one considers the (infinite) matrix \\(H = (h_{\\kappa\\lambda})\\), with \\(h_{\\kappa\\lambda} =h(p_\\kappa^\\lambda)\\). If every entry occurs in \\(H\\) only a finite number of times, then there exists a purely (but not absolutely) periodic sequence \\(\\{A_\\nu\\}\\) of period \\(h(m)\\) modulo \\(m\\). \n\nTo given \\(h(m)\\) one considers the set \\(\\mathfrak M = \\mathfrak M(h(m))\\) of sequences that are purely periodic and admit the period \\(h = h(m)\\) modulo \\(m\\). \n\nTheorem: To each set \\(\\mathfrak M\\) there exists a basis \\(\\{\\mathfrak F_j\\}\\), i.e., sequences \\(\\mathfrak F = \\{A_\\nu\\}\\) such that every sequence \\(\\mathfrak F\\in\\mathfrak M\\) can be represented as \\(\\mathfrak F= \\sum_{j=0}^\\infty z_j \\mathfrak F_j\\), \\(z_j\\in\\mathbb Z\\). The integers \\(z_j\\) are uniquely determined by \\(\\mathfrak F\\). The basis is finite only when \\(h(m)\\) is bounded, i.e., when \\(\\mathfrak M\\) consists only of absolutely periodic sequences. Any basis may be normalized to triangular form \\(\\mathfrak F_\\mu = \\{d_{\\mu\\nu}\\}\\), \n\\[ \nd_{\\mu\\nu} = 0\\text{ for }\\mu \u003e \\nu, 0\u003cd_{\\mu\\mu}, d_{\\mu\\mu}\\mid d_{\\mu+1,\\mu+1}, d_{\\mu\\mu}\\mid d_{\\mu\\nu}\\ (\\nu\\ge \\mu). \n\\] \n\nChapter 7 discusses further properties of bases for \\(\\mathfrak M\\) and gives many examples. While the \\(z_j\\)\u0027s are uniquely determined by \\(\\mathfrak F\\), the \\(\\mathfrak F_j\\) (even normalized) are not uniquely determined by \\(\\mathfrak M\\). Typical examples: For \\(h(m) = m\\), \\(\\left\\{M(n)\\binom{\\nu}{n}\\right\\}\\) \\((\\nu = 0,1, \\ldots)\\) form a basis. For \\(h(m) = m^k\\), a basis is furnished by \n\\[ \n\\mathfrak F_n = \\left\\{M(n^{1/k})\\binom{\\nu}{n}\\right\\}\\quad (M(x) = M([x])). \n\\] \n\nCorollary: For all integers \\(k,m,n\\), \\(M(n^{1/k})\\binom{m^k-1}{n-1}\\frac{m^{k-1}}{n}\\) is an integer. \n\nThe proofs are elementary, although not trivial, or even always easy. Some of the ideas, especially of the first three chapters seem to be related to similar ones in [\\textit{C. Pisot}, Ann. Sc. Norm. Super. Pisa, II. Ser. 7, 205--248 (1938; Zbl 0019.15502), see also Thesis, Paris (1938; Zbl 0019.00703); see also his lecture notes from the University of Montreal (1963; Zbl 0141.04701)].",

                                            "text":  "The authors investigate periodicity of expansions in alternate base systems. A Cantor real base system is a representation of real numbers \\(x\\in[0, 1)\\) as\n\\[\nx = \\sum_{k=1}^\\infty \\frac{x_k}{\\prod_{i=1}^k\\beta_i}\n\\]\nwith \\(x_k\\in\\mathbb{N}\\) where \\(\\mathcal{B}=(\\beta_i)_{i\\ge 1}\\) with \\(\\beta_i\u003e1\\) for all \\(i\\). If \\(\\mathcal{B}\\) is purely periodic with period of length \\(p\\), \\(\\mathcal{B}\\) is called an alternate base and we write \\(\\mathcal{B}=(\\beta_1,\\ldots,\\beta_p)\\). The quantity \\(\\delta= \\prod_{i=1}^p \\beta_i\\) will occur frequently in the results of this paper.\n\nThe set \\(\\operatorname{Per}(\\mathcal{B})\\) is defined to be the set of numbers in the unit interval \\([0, 1)\\) with periodic expansion in the alternate base number system defined by \\(\\mathcal{B}\\). An alternate base \\(\\mathcal{B}\\) is said to satisfy the pure periodicity property if there exists an interval \\([0, \\gamma)\\) with \\(0\u003c\\gamma\\le 1\\) such that every rational in \\([0, \\gamma)\\) has a purely periodic \\(\\mathcal{B}\\) expansion. Finally, we say that \\(\\mathcal{B}\\) has the finiteness property if adding and subtracting finite \\(\\mathcal{B}\\) expansions again yields finite \\(\\mathcal{B}\\) expansions.\n\nExtending previous results and proving a conjecture by \\textit{É. Charlier} et al. [J. Number Theory 254, 184--198 (2024; Zbl 1536.11120)], the authors show that for an alternate base \\(\\mathcal{B}\\) if \\(\\mathbb{Q}\\cap [0, 1)\\subseteq \\operatorname{Per}(\\mathcal{B})\\), then \\(\\delta\\) is either a Pisot or a Salem number and \\(\\beta_1\\), \\dots, \\(\\beta_p\\in\\mathbb{Q}(\\delta)\\).\n\nNext, the authors prove that if \\(\\mathcal{B}\\) is an alternate base with the pure periodicity property, then \\(\\delta\\) is a Pisot or a Salem unit, \\(\\beta_1\\), \\dots, \\(\\beta_p\\in\\mathbb{Q}(\\delta)\\), and the vector \\((\\psi(\\beta_1), \\ldots, \\psi(\\beta_p))\\) is not positive for any non-identical embedding \\(\\psi\\colon \\mathbb{Q}(\\delta)\\to\\mathbb{C}\\).\n\nFinally, the authors prove a partial converse: if \\(\\mathcal{B}\\) is an alternate base with the finiteness property such that \\(\\delta\\) is a Pisot unit, then \\(\\mathcal{B}\\) as well as all of its cyclic shifts satisfy the pure periodicity property.",

                                            "text":  "Let \\(a,b,g\\) be positive integers with \\(a\u003cb,\\; \\gcd(a,b) = 1\\) and \\(g \\geq 2\\). If the \\(g\\)-ary expansion of \\(a/b = x_1g^{-1} + x_2g^{-2} + \\ldots\\) (denoted by \\(0.x_1x_2\\ldots\\)) is eventually periodic with preperiod \\(0.x_1\\ldots x_{i_0}\\) and shortest period \\(n\\), we call \\(x_{i_0+1}\\ldots x_{i+n}\\) the repetend of the expansion of \\(a/b\\).\n\nThe authors prove (Theorem 2) that if the \\(g\\)-ary expansion of \\(a/b^{k+t} = x_1g^{-1} + x_2g^{-2} + \\ldots\\) is purely periodic, then for every \\(j \\geq 1\\), every possible word (of the alphabet \\(\\{0,\\ldots, g-1\\}\\)) of length \\(j\\) appears in the repetend of \\(a/b^{k+t}\\) with a relative frequency that converges to \\(1/g^j\\) as \\(t \\to \\infty\\).\n\nThis result is generalized in Theorem 3: Let \\((a_k)_{k \\in \\mathbb{N}}\\) be a sequence of positive integers coprime to \\(b\\). Sadahiro} [Integers 9, No. 3, 239--259, A22 (2009; Zbl 1191.11005)] definiert und auf ihre grundlegenden Eigenschaften untersucht wurden. Für reelle \\(\\beta\u003e1\\) ist dabei \\(I_\\beta\\) das Intervall \\([-\\beta/(\\beta+1),1/(\\beta+1))\\) und die \\((-\\beta)\\)-Transformation \\(T_{-\\beta} \\colon I_\\beta\\to I_\\beta\\) ist gegeben durch \n\\[\nT_{-\\beta}(x)=-\\beta x-\\lfloor -\\beta x+\\beta/(\\beta+1)\\rfloor.\n\\]\n Zuerst behandeln Verff. das Problem, ob es ein Intervall \\(J\\subset I_\\beta\\) mit \\(0\\in J\\) gibt derart, dass jedes \\(x\\in\\mathbb{Q}\\cap J\\) eine rein-periodische \\((-\\beta)\\)-Entwicklung besitzt. An der Vorgehensweise im Fall positiver Basen orientiert beweisen sie: Eine notwendige Bedingung für die Existenz eines solchen \\(J\\) ist, dass \\(\\beta\\) eine ganze algebraische Einheit ist, die entweder Pisot- oder Salem-Zahl ist. Als hinreichende Bedingung erweist sich hier: \\(\\beta\\) ist Pisot-Einheit mit der Eigenschaft, dass \\(\\text{Fin}(-\\beta)\\), die Menge der endlichen \\((-\\beta)\\)-Entwicklungen, mit \\(\\mathbb{Z}[\\beta]\\) zusammenfällt und der linke Endpunkt von \\(I_\\beta\\) eine unendliche Entwicklung hat. Weiter wird der Fall quadratischer Pisot-Einheiten diskutiert, wobei das Intervall \\(J\\) bei positiver bzw. negativer Konjugierten (von \\(\\beta\\)) gesondert beschrieben wird. Schließlich wird gezeigt, dass im Fall quadratischer \\(\\beta\\) die Bedingung \\(\\text{Fin}(-\\beta)=\\mathbb{Z} [\\beta]\\) für die Existenz eines \\(J\\) wie oben nicht notwendig ist.",

                                            "text":  "Continuing their earlier paper [Ann. Math. (2) 165, No. 2, 547--565 (2007; Zbl 1195.11094)] the authors prove two theorems giving Diophantine criteria for transcendence applying Schmidt\u0027s subspace theorem. \n\nLet \\(\\mathbf a=\\{a_l\\}_{l\\geq 1}\\) be a sequence of elements from a (not necessarily finite) set \\(\\mathcal A\\), that we identify with the infinite word \\(a_1a_2\\dots a_l \\dots\\). Let \\(w\\) be a rational number with \\(w\u003e1\\). \\(\\mathbf a\\) is said to satisfy Condition \\((*)_w\\) if \\(\\mathbf a\\) is not eventually periodic and if there exists a sequence of finite words \\(\\{V_n\\}_{n\\geq 1}\\) such that (i) for \\(n\\geq 1\\), the word \\(V_n^w\\) is a prefix of the word \\(\\mathbf a\\); (ii) the sequence \\(\\{V_n\\}_{n\\geq 1}\\) is increasing.\n\nFirst a transcendence criterion for `purely\u0027 stammering continued fractions is given as follows:\n\nTheorem 1. Let \\(\\mathbf a=\\{a_l\\}_{l\\geq 1}\\) be a sequence of positive integers. Let \\(\\{pz/qz\\}_{l\\geq 1}\\) denote the sequence of convergents to the real number \\(\\alpha:= [0; a_1, a_2, \\dots, a_l,\\dots]\\). If there exists a rational number \\(w\\geq 2\\) such that a satisfies Condition \\((*)_w\\), then a is transcendental. If there exists a rational number \\(w\u003e1\\) such that a satisfies Condition \\((*)_w\\), and if the sequence \\(\\{q_l^{1/l}\\}_{l\\geq 1}\\) is bounded (which is, in particular, the case when the sequence \\(\\mathbf a\\) is bounded), then \\(\\alpha\\) is transcendental.\n\nThe main interest of the first statement of Theorem 1 is that there is no condition on the growth of the sequence \\(\\{q_l\\}_{l\\geq 1}\\). The second statement of Theorem 1 improves upon Theorem 4 from [\\textit{J.-P. Allouche} et al., J. Number Theory 91, 39--66 (2001)],\nwhich requires, together with some extra rather constraining hypotheses, the stronger assumption \\(w\u003e3/2\\). The condition that the sequence \\(\\{q_l^{1/l}\\}_{l\\geq 1}\\) has to be bounded is in general easy to check, and is not very restrictive, since it is satisfied by almost\nall real numbers (in the sense of the Lebesgue measure). Apart from this assumption, Theorem 1 does not depend on the size of the partial quotients of \\(\\alpha\\). This is in a striking contrast to all previous results.\n\nThen Theorem 2 gives a transcendence criterion for (general) stammering continued fractions.\n\nLet \\(\\mathbf a\\) be as in Theorem 1. Let \\(\\{p_l/q_l\\}_{l\\geq 1}\\) denote\nthe sequence of convergents to the real number \\(\\alpha:= [0; a_1, a_2, \\dots, a_l,\\dots]\\). Assume that the sequence \\(\\{q_l^{1/l}\\}_{l\\geq 1}\\) is bounded and set \\(M=\\limsup_{l\\to +infty} q_l^{1/l}\\) and \\(m=\\liminf_{l\\to +infty} q_l^{1/l}\\). Let \\(w\\) and \\(w\u0027\\) be non-negative real numbers with \n\\[\nw \u003e (2w\u0027+1) \\frac{\\log M}{\\log m}-w\u0027.\n\\]\n If \\(\\mathbf a\\) satisfies Condition \\((**)_{w,w\u0027}\\) (similar to \\((*)_w\\) above), then \\(\\alpha\\) is transcendental.\n\nSeveral applications of these theorems are then briefly discussed.",

                                            "text":  "Let \\(\\beta\\) be a Pisot number and let \\(x\\) be a real number in \\([0,1).\\) \\textit{K. Schmidt} [Bull. Lond. Math. Soc. 12, 269--278 (1980; Zbl 0494.10040)] proved that \\(x \\in {\\mathbb Q}(\\beta)\\) if and only if the \\(\\beta\\)-greedy expansion of \\(x\\) is periodic. \\textit{S. Ito} and \\textit{Y. Sano} [Osaka J. Math. 38, 349--368 (2001; Zbl 0991.11040)] found an `if and only if\u0027 condition on \\(x\\) for its \\(\\beta\\)-greedy expansion to be purely periodic in case that \\(\\beta\\) is a cubic Pisot number. It depends on two other conjugates of \\(x.\\) In this paper the author proves a similar result for all Pisot numbers \\(\\beta.\\) More precisely, he shows that \\(x\\) has a purely periodic \\(\\beta\\)-expansion if and only if \\(x \\in {\\mathbb Q}(\\beta)\\) is reduced. The definition of a reduced real algebraic number is quite technical: it is given in terms of its minimal polynomial and of its conjugates over \\({\\mathbb Q}.\\)",

                                            "text":  "A (weak) form of Midy\u0027s theorem reads as follows: Let \\(q \u003e 5\\) be a prime number. If the minimal period of a rational number \\(p/q \\in (0, 1)\\) has even length, then the sum of the first and the second halves of the period is a number whose expansion in the decimal system uses only the digit \\(9\\). This is a quite astonishing result. In particular, as the authors write: ``[...] this result can serve for the general public as an illustration that mathematics can simply be fun.\u0027\u0027\n\nWhile several authors have given generalizations of this theorem, the paper under review studies the corresponding question when integer numeration bases are replaced with non-integer bases \\(\\beta\\) (à la Rényi). The authors say that \\(q \\in {\\mathbb N}\\) has the Midy property in base \\(\\beta \u003e 1\\) if there exists a positive integer \\(p \u003c q\\) coprime with q such that\n\\begin{itemize}\n\\item[(i)] the \\(\\beta\\)-expansion of \\(p/q\\) is purely periodic: \\((p/q)_{\\beta} = 0.(c_1 c_2\\dots c_{2n})^{\\omega}\\) where \\(2n\\) is the length of the shortest period;\n\\item[(ii)] \\(x + y = \\beta^n - 1,\\) where \\(x, y\\) are \\(\\beta\\)-integers with \\(\\beta\\)-expansions \\((x)_{\\beta} = c_1c_2\\cdots c_n\\) and \\((y)_{\\beta} = c_{n+1}c_{n+2}\\dots c_{2n}\\), respectively.\n\\end{itemize}\nThe number \\(p\\) is then said to testify to the Midy property of \\(q\\) in base \\(\\beta\\).\n\nFirst the authors give a necessary condition for an integer \\(q \u003e 2\\) to have the Midy property in base \\(\\beta\\), where \\(\\beta \u003e 1\\) is an algebraic integer: this condition involves the companion matrix of \\(\\beta\\). The condition is not sufficient, but the authors prove that it is sufficient when the base is the golden ratio \\(\\frac{1+\\sqrt{5}}{2}\\). Then they prove for example that all primes \\(q\\) such that either \\(q=5\\) or \\(q \\equiv \\pm 2 \\bmod 5\\) have the Midy property in the golden ratio base. The proofs of the various results given in the paper are reasonably elementary but ingenious.",
                                            "contribution_type":  "review"

                                            "text":  "A circle of results and questions in dynamics and number theory are concerned with the special properties of Pisot numbers, and in many cases there is an underlying substitution system built on a finite alphabet. Here there is a standard conjecture, formulated in this paper as asking if the tiling flow associated with a one-dimensional substitution of unimodular irreducible Pisot type has pure discrete spectrum. Here the authors introduce a notion of homological Pisot substitutions, namely one-dimensional substitution tiling spaces whose dilation factor is a degree \\(d\\) Pisot number with the property that the first rational Čech homology is \\(d\\)-dimensional. Examples of such substitutions are found with tiling flows whose spectrum is not pure discrete. The examples constructed are not unimodular, and it is conjectured here that the coincidence rank must divide a power of the norm of the dilation. Evidence is given to support this conjecture via constraints arising from the dynamics on the possible measures of cylinder sets in the corresponding tiling space.",

                                            "text":  "Summary: We consider the structure of Pisot substitution tiling spaces, in particular, the structure of those spaces for which the translation action does not have pure discrete spectrum. Such a space is always a measurable \\(m\\)-to-one cover of an action by translation on a group called the maximal equicontinuous factor. The integer \\(m\\) is the coincidence rank of the substitution and equals one if and only if translation on the tiling space has pure discrete spectrum. By considering factors intermediate between a tiling space and its maximal equicontinuous factor, we establish a lower bound on the cohomology of a one-dimensional Pisot substitution tiling space with coincidence rank two and dilation of odd norm. The Coincidence Rank Conjecture, for coincidence rank two, is a corollary.",

                                            "text":  "Summary: This paper surveys different constructions and properties of some multiple tilings (that\nis, finite-to-one coverings) of the space that can be associated with beta-numeration and substitutions. It is indeed possible, generalizing Rauzy\u0027s and Thurston\u0027s constructions, to associate in a natural way either with a Pisot number \\(\\beta\\) (of degree \\(d\\)) or with a Pisot substitution \\(\\sigma\\) (on \\(d\\) letters) some compact basic tiles that are the closure of their interior, that have non-zero measure and a fractal boundary; they are attractors of some graphdirected Iterated Function System. We know that some translates of these prototiles under a Delone set~\\(\\Gamma\\) (provided by \\(\\beta\\) or \\(\\sigma\\)) cover \\(\\mathbb R^{d-1}\\); it is conjectured that this multiple tiling is indeed a tiling (which might be either periodic or self-replicating according to the translation set \\(\\Gamma\\)). This conjecture is known as the Pisot conjecture and can also be reformulated in spectral terms: the associated dynamical systems have pure discrete spectrum. We detail here the known constructions for these tilings, their main properties, some applications, and focus on some equivalent formulations of the Pisot conjecture, in the theory of quasicrystals for instance. We state in particular for Pisot substitutions a finiteness property analogous to the well-known (F) property in beta-numeration, which is a sufficient condition to get a tiling.\n\nThis paper also contains a valuable bibliography.",

                                            "text":  "The authors deal with the Pisot substitution conjecture. They show that the subshift associated to an irreducible Pisot substitution has pure discrete spectrum as soon as the interior of a piece of the discrete line is non-empty. \n\nThe authors present the main general geometric criterion for a subshift to have a pure discrete spectrum. Let \\(s\\) be an irreducible unit Pisot substitution over an alphabet \\(A\\), and let \\(u \\in A^{\\mathbb{N}}\\) be a periodic point of \\(s\\). In this case, they prove that the subshift \\((\\overline{S^{\\mathbb{N}}u}, S)\\) has pure discrete spectrum if and only if \\(\\exists a\\in A\\), \\(\\overset{\\circ}{D}_{u,a}\\neq \\emptyset\\). Then, they present a way to investigate the Pisot substitution conjecture for any given irreducible Pisot unit substitution. It is proven that a certain condition is equivalent to the non-emptiness of some computable regular language. For every word \\(s_0s_1 \\cdots \\in \\mathcal{S}^{\\mathbb{N}}\\), the authors prove that the subshift \\((\\overline{S^{\\mathbb{N}}u}, S)\\) is measurably isomorphic to a translation on a torus, where \\(\\mathcal{S}^{\\mathbb{N}}=\\{\\sigma,\\tau\\}\\), \\(\\sigma\\) and \\(\\tau\\) are two substitutions over the alphabet \\(A = \\{a, b, c\\}\\).\n\nFor the entire collection see [Zbl 1454.37001].",

                                            "text":  "Self similar substitutive systems are shift invariant symbolic dynamical systems generated by the fixed point of a letter replacing rule, namely a substitution. Rauzy, Thurston, Arnoux-Ito stressed out the relation between these symbolic dynamical systems with self-similar dynamical systems such as hyperbolic toral automorphisms or numeration systems in noninteger basis. When the automorphism as a one-dimensional expanding direction, that is, the dominant eigenvalue is a Pisot number, the set of eigenvalues of the system includes the eigenvalues a toral translation. The question known as the Pisot conjecture or GCC asks whether the system is indeed measure-theoretically isomorphic with a toral translation. In 2006, the Pisot conjecture was proved to be equivalent to a combinatorial condition named the geometric condition (see the authors\u0027 paper in [(1) Am. J. Math. 128, No. 5, 1219-1282 (2006; Zbl 1152.37011)] and a paper from \\textit{S. Ito} and \\textit{H. Rao} [Isr. J. Math. 153, 129--155 (2006). The proof of (1) is a part of a larger formalism starting from a substitution to define a flow on a real space. \n\nThe first part of the present paper intends to proved a summary of the main concepts and proofs of (1). In the second part, the authors prove that the GCC conjecture is satisfied by a class of beta-substitutions, where beta is a simple Parry number with prime degree and negative coefficients in its mimimal polynomial. This generalizes several results from Frougny-Solomyak and Akiyama-Rao-Steiner.\n\nFor the entire collection see [Zbl 1075.37001].",

                                                         },
                                            "text":  "A substitution subshift is one generated by the sequence obtained as the limit of images of the string ``1\u0027\u0027 via iterates of a substitution rule \\(\\zeta:\\mathcal A\\to\\mathcal A^*\\), where \\(\\mathcal A = \\{1,2,\\dots,d\\}\\) is called alphabet, \\(\\mathcal A^* = \\bigcup_{n\\geq 1} \\mathcal A^n\\), and \\(\\zeta(1) = 1B\\), \\(B\\in\\mathcal A^*\\). The substitution \\(\\zeta\\) is of Pisot type if the Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue \\(\\lambda\\) of the associated matrix \\(M_\\zeta\\) (with entries \\(m_{i,j}\\) equal to the number of occurrences of the symbol \\(i\\) in \\(\\zeta(j)\\)) is a Pisot number and the characteristic polynomial of \\(M_\\zeta\\) is irreducible; in other words, all eigenvalues other than \\(\\lambda\\) are of modulus strictly less than one.\n\nThere is a long standing conjecture that every substitution subshift of Pisot type has a pure discrete spectrum. This conjecture has been proved true by \\textit{M. Barge} and \\textit{B. Diamond} [Bull. Soc. Math. Fr. 130, 619--626 (2002; Zbl 1028.37008)] for the case of two symbols.\n\nPresented (with a new proof) is a version of so-called ``balanced pairs algorithm\u0027\u0027 of \\textit{A. N. Livshits} [Russ. Math. Surv. 42, 222--223 (1987; Zbl 0648.47004)], allowing one to test for a pure discrete spectrum in substitution subshifts.\n\nThen, the authors provide conditions for a pure discrete spectrum of the tiling flow associated to a substitution subshift of Pisot type, obtained as the suspension over the subshift with the height function constant on each zero-coordinate cylinder and equal to the corresponding coordinate of the Perron-Frobenius eigenvector. They employ the ``overlap algorithm\u0027\u0027 introduced formerly by the second author for two-dimensional tilings [Ergodic Theory Dyn. Syst. 17, 695--738 (1997; Zbl 0884.58062)], and prove an equivalence between certain behavior of this algorithm and a certain behavior of the balanced pairs algorithm. As result, they deduce that pure point spectrum of the tiling flow implies pure point spectrum of the substitution subshift, and that, in the two-symbol case, the tiling flow has a pure point spectrum (in particular, covering the result of Barge and Diamond).\n\nIt must be noted (as the authors do), that a stronger result has been recently proved by \\textit{A. Clark} and \\textit{L. Sadun} [Ergodic Theory Dyn. Syst. 23, 1043--1057 (2003; Zbl 1042.37008)] for substitutions of Pisot type: pure point spectrum of the flow is equivalent to pure point spectrum of the subshift.\n\nThe paper is concluded with an appendix containing four examples with the balanced pairs algorithm conducted using MATHEMATICA (and testing positive for a pure point spectrum).",
                                            "contribution_type":  "review"
                                        }

                                            "text":  "Summary: This thesis consists (mainly) of three parts: At first, we define Hausdorff measures for product spaces of local fields. We look at iterated function systems on such spaces, the Hausdorff dimension of their attractor is estimated. Afterwards, model sets (respectively cut and project sets) are introduced. For point sets generated by a substitution rule, we state criteria that ensure that the point set in question is a model set. These results are applied to Pisot substitutions. It is conjectured that all (one-dimensional) point sets generated by a Pisot substitution are model sets. A list of equivalent statements for this conjecture is given.\nIn the first part of Chapter 4 we show that the Haar measure on a product space of local fields is a Hausdorff measure (Theorem 4.56). Then, iterated function systems and their attractors are introduced. Generalising results of K. J. Falconer (on \\(R^n\\)), upper (Prop. 4.122) and in some cases lower (Lemma 4.126 \\\u0026 Props. 4.127 \\\u0026 4.129) bounds for the Hausdorff dimension (as well as the box-counting dimension (Lemma 4.133)) for these attractors are derived.\n\nThe main theme of Chapter 5 are model sets (cut and project sets) and Delone point sets that are generated by a substitution, and their interplay. Following Baake-Moody, the construction of a cut and project scheme for a multi-component Delone set is derived in Section 5.3. This construction is extended and modified for substitution point sets (Section 5.7.3) if there is a so-called algebraic or overlap coincidence; indeed, one obtains an extended internal space here (Prop. 5.137). The main theorem of this chapter is Theorem 5.154 which states equivalent conditions under which a substitution point set is a model set: Either the substitution has an algebraic or overlap coincidence, or there exist certain aperiodic tilings of the (extended) internal space.\n\nThese results are applied to sequences generated by Pisot substitutions in Chapter 6 (Theorem 6.77). However, one can derive additional equivalent conditions, e.g., that a certain periodic tiling of the internal space exists (Prop. 6.72), or that the so-called ``Geometric Coincidence Condition\u0027\u0027 (GCC) is satisfied (for the latter, we also state a graph-theoretic formulation, see Section 6.9). The complete list -- and thus the central theorem of this thesis -- of all equivalent conditions is given in Theorem 6.116. Here, we have also included statements from Chapter 7. In that chapter, we mainly summarise results about the diffraction measure of Delone sets, the spectrum of the dynamical system generated by a Delone set and the torus parametrisation for a model set already present in the literature.\nTo contextualize the achieved results, we look at and apply our methods to ``visible lattice points\u0027\u0027 (Chapter 5a), tilings of the plane (Chapter 6a), lattice substitution systems (Chapter 6b) and reducible Pisot substitutions and [beta]-substitutions (Chapter 6c).",
                                            "contribution_type":  "summary"

                                            "text":  "The first basic result in the theory of the Riemann zeta function \\(\\zeta(s)=\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} n^{-s}=\\prod_{p}\\left(1-p^{-s}\\right)^{-1}\\) is that it can be analytically continued to the whole plane except for a simple pole at \\(s=1\\) and satifies a so called functional equation, which says that the function \\(\\pi^{-s/2} \\Gamma(s/2) \\zeta(s)\\) is invariant under the substitution \\(s \\leftrightarrow 1-s\\). In studying varieties defined over a global field \\(K\\), one may construct functions by means of product formulas similar to the one for \\(\\zeta(s)\\). These functions are called the zeta functions of the varieties. The Hasse-Weil conjecture is that for nonsingular projective varieties these functions again have an analytic continuation and a functional equation (which will be somewhat more complicated). The conjecture has been verified for various restricted families of varieties, but until now no one has written down even a conjectured form for the functional equation in general. This is just what the author does in this paper. \n\nIn addition to finding the analogues for \\(\\pi^{-s/2}\\) and \\(\\Gamma(s/2)\\) in the functional equation for \\(\\zeta(s)\\) (these do turn out to have the form, respectively, \\(A^s\\), some \\(A\u003e0\\), and a product of gamma functions), one also encounters difficulty in getting the right factors in the product formula for certain primes which are exceptional for the variety (the primes at which the variety has ``bad reduction\u0027\u0027). The other slight modifications necessary for the general functional equation (for example, a shift in the line of symmetry) are already suggested unambiguously by known results. \n\nWhat is of interest in this paper is, of course, seeing which elements of structure play a role in defining each of the extra factors, as well as following the author\u0027s reasoning by analogy from the cases in wich the form of the functional equation is known, the central example here being abelian varieties with sufficiently many complex multiplications. First of all, modulo a number of preliminary conjectures, of quite considerable interest themselves, to the effect that the \\(\\ell\\)-adic cohomology of a nonsingular projective variety over \\(K\\) is, as a Galois module, as well-behaved as it is in the case of abelian varieties, the author produces for each bad prime a well-defined factor for the product formula (gotten from the characteristic polynomial of the inverse of the Frobenius acting where it can -- namely on the subspace of the cohomology invariant under the inertia group). The author then defines the gamma factors in terms of the Hodge decomposition of the underlying complex manifold corresponding to each archimedean prime in \\(K\\). Here, however, reasoning by analogy from abelian varieties is less convincing -- the Hodge decomposition and gamma-factors are too simple. For lack of a more interesting example, the appeal to the Hodge decomposition looks like just a shot in the dark. (To be sure, Serre\u0027s marksmanship is uncanny.) Whereas the author incorporates in a natural way the \\(\\pi^{-8/2}\\) factor for the functional equation for \\( \\zeta(s) \\) into his definition of the gamma factors, the need to define a factor of the form \\(A^8\\) persists, as one knows from examples. As expected, \\(A\\) depends on the discriminant of \\(K\\) and the ``conductor\u0027\u0027. (This latter measures the ``badness\u0027\u0027 of the bad primes. The author gives a general definition for it in terms of the Galois module structure of the l-adic cohomology, conjecturing that indeed it doesn\u0027t depend on \\(\\ell\\).) \n\nAs essential new evidence for the conjectures (in fact, as he says, partly the basis for them), the author announces a new functional equation proved by Grothendieck for varieties over global fields of positive characteristic.",

                                            "text":  "Heuristics say that an irrational real number whose sequence of digits in its base-2 expansion has some kind of regularity, then it is transcendental. In particular, \\textit{J. Loxton} and \\textit{A. J. van der Poorten} state in [J. Reine Angew. Math. 392, 57-69 (1988; Zbl 0656.10033)] that the digits in the \\(k\\)-ary expansion of an algebraic irrational number cannot be generated by a finite \\(k\\)-automaton (note that this result should be considered as a conjecture since there is still a gap in their proof).\n\n\nThe paper under review proves that a positive real number whose binary expansion is a fixed point of a non-trivial morphism (over \\(\\{0,1\\}\\)) which is either of constant length or primitive, must be rational or transcendental. This paper is a continuation of [\\textit{S. Ferenczi} and \\textit{C. Mauduit}, J. Number Theory 67, 146-161 (1997; Zbl 0895.11029)] and uses a combinatorial translation of a transcendence criterium due to Ridout, given in this last paper: if the expansion in some basis of an irrational number contains infinitely may \\(2+\\varepsilon\\)-powers of blocks at distances from the origin which are not too much larger than the lengths of the considered blocks, then it is transcendental. In the case of the fixed point of a primitive or of a non-trivial constant length morphism, this criterium reduces to the existence of overlaps. \\textit{P. Séébold} [Discrete Appl. Math. 11, 255-264 (1985; Zbl 0583.20047)] gave a description of the overlap-free fixed points of non-trivial morphisms (these are the two fixed points of the Thue-Morse substitution). Since the Thue-Morse number is known to be transcendental, this completes the proof of the paper under review.",

                                            "text":  "Aperiodic order is a topic of general interest to the study of tiling theory, dynamical systems, topology, ergodic theory, computer graphics and mathematical physics. The work of \\textit{J. E. Anderson} and \\textit{I. F. Putnam} [Ergodic Theory Dyn. Syst. 18, No. 3, 509--537 (1998; Zbl 1053.46520)] has led to a new algebraic topological approach to the study of aperiodic sequences and tilings associated with substitutions. The Pisot conjecture says that the subshift of every irreducible Pisot substitution has pure discrete spectrum, and the strong coincidence conjecture says that every irreducible Pisot substitution is strongly coincident.\n\nIn this paper, the authors provide a survey of results from symbolic dynamics and algebraic topology revisited with \\textit{Grout} which is a new user-friendly program developed to calculate combinatorial properties and topological invariants of a large class of symbolic substitutions. They also give a brief overview of results related to the Pisot conjecture and the strong coincidence conjecture and verify that no counterexample exists to the strong coincidence conjecture for a large number of substitutions on three and four letters.",

                                            "text":  "The authors consider the balanced pair algorithm for Rauzy fractals and its applicability. In particular, they prove that given two primitive, unimodular Pisot substitutions \\(\\zeta_1\\) and \\(\\zeta_2\\) with the same incidence matrix satisfying the strong coincidence condition and inducing a proper lattice tiling, the balanced pair algorithm of \\(\\zeta_1\\) and \\(\\zeta_2\\) is defined and terminates iff the interior of the intersection of the associated Rauzy fractals is nonempty. In addition, the authors give necessary conditions based only on the spectral properties of the incidence matrix of the substitution that guarantee that the substitution does not have the geometric property (F), i.e., that the Rauzy fractal contains the origin as an interior point.",

                                            "text":  "Summary: The matrix of a substitution is not sufficient to completely determine the dynamics associated with it, even in the simplest cases since there are many words with the same abelianization. In this paper we study the common points of the canonical broken lines associated with two different irreducible Pisot unimodular substitutions \\(\\sigma_1\\) and \\(\\sigma_2\\) having the same incidence matrix. We prove that if 0 is an inner point of the Rauzy fractal associated with the substitution \\(\\sigma_1\\) and \\(\\sigma_1\\) verifies the Pisot conjecture then these common points can be generated with a substitution on an alphabet of so-called balanced pairs, and we obtain in this way the intersection of the interior of two Rauzy fractals.",

                                            "text":  "The modern theory of aperiodic tilings started in the beginning of the 1960s, with the proof by Berger of the undecidability of the ``domino problem\u0027\u0027, using aperiodic tilings, followed by the invention of the Penrose tiling, the ``heighway dragon\u0027\u0027 and the ``Knuth-Davis twindragon\u0027\u0027, soon followed by the discovery of quasi-crystals and the study of tiling spaces, which are a basic example of noncommutative geometry. Self-similar tilings, like the Fibonacci and Penrose tilings, were fundamental objects of this development and over time they have been generalized in many ways.\n\nThis book is the presentation of several recent developments in the study of aperiodic tilings, and contains lecture notes by several authors delivered at the research school ``Tiling Dynamical Systems\u0027\u0027, one of the Morlet Chair events organized in the second semester of 2017 as part of the program ``Tilings and Discrete Geometry\u0027\u0027.\n\nThe synopsis of the book goes as follows.\n\nChapter 1 aims to supplement the lectures of N. P. Frank (in Chapter 2), focusing on selected topics such as Delone sets as models for quasicrystals, inflation symmetries and expansion constants, substitution Delone sets and tilings, and associated dynamical systems.\n\nChapter 2 is concerned with the tiling dynamical systems approach to the study of aperiodic order, comparing four types of systems, namely, one-dimensional symbolic systems, one-dimensional tiling systems, multidimensional \\(\\mathbb{Z}^{d}\\)-systems and multidimensional tiling sytems.\n\nChapter 3 is concerned with Sturmian sequences, which are infinite nonperiodic strings over two letters with minimal subword complexity. The author (Jörg M. Thurswaldner) explains the ideas in [\\textit{V. Berthé} et al., Ann. Inst. Fourier 69, No. 3, 1347--1409 (2019; Zbl 1433.37010)], where, using a generalization of \\textit{G. Rauzy}\u0027s induction process [Acta Arith. 34, 315--328 (1979; Zbl 0414.28018)], it is proved that under certain natural conditions an \\(S\\)-adic sequence gives rise to a dynamical system which is measurably conjugate to a rotation on a higher dimensional torus.\n\nChapter 4 reviews the construction of operators and algebras from tilings of Euclidean space. It is explained how the physical notion of locality of interaction is related to the mathematical notion of pattern equivalence for tilings and how this leads naturally to the definition of tiling algebras. The author (Johannes Kellendonk) gives a brief introduction to the \\(K\\)-theory of tiling algebras, exposing how the algebraic topology of \\(K\\)-theory gives rise to a correspondence between the topological invariants of the bulk and its boundary of a material.\n\nChapter 5 presents some of the existing connections between combinatorial game theory and combinatorics on words, regarding multidimensional infinite words as tilings of \\(\\mathbb{N}^{d}\\), which naturally arise from subtraction games on \\(d\\)\\ heaps of tokens.\n\nChapter 6 explains that the undecidability of the ``domino problem\u0027\u0027 [see \\url{https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6773658}] has as a consequence the existence of an aperiodic tileset.\n\nChapter 7 employs the geometric inflation rule to access the pair correlation measures of self-similar and self-affine inflation tilings and their Fourier transforms by means of exact renormalization relations, looking into sufficient criteria for the absence of absolutely continuous spectral contributions and illustrating this with examples from the class of block substitutions. The Frank-Robinson tiling (see [\\textit{N. Priebe Frank} and \\textit{E. A. Robinson jun.}, Trans. Am. Math. Soc. 360, No. 3, 1163--1177 (2008; Zbl 1138.37010)]) is also addressed as a planar example with infinite local complexity and singular continuous spectrum.\n\nChapter 8 provides a sufficient geometric condition for a subshift to be measurably isomorphic to a domain exchange and to a translation on a torus, which gives another characterization of the Pisot substitution conjecture (see [\\textit{S. Akiyama} et al., Prog. Math. 309, 33--72 (2015; Zbl 1376.37043)]).",
